# Abstract

Interaction is invoked across human-computer interaction, cybernetics,
ecology, cognitive science, communication, control, formal methods,
robotics, and multi-agent systems, but these traditions do not share a
single definition. Some identify interaction with reciprocal action,
some with communication, some with feedback, some with synchronized
events, and some with situated meaning-making. This paper tests whether
interaction is primitive or reducible to established constructs. It
concludes that interaction is not a primitive substance or basic event
type. It is a higher-order relation over coupled processes: two or more
distinguishable systems interact during an episode when changes in each
system\'s possible or actual state trajectory are counterfactually
dependent on perturbations transmitted through a coupling relation
within a declared boundary and timescale. Reciprocity may be asymmetric,
delayed, mediated, probabilistic, or realized across a sequence;
simultaneous action, intention, communication, semantic understanding,
and visible behavior are not necessary. A single unilateral causal
effect is insufficient unless it enters a closed or recurrent dependency
structure. Existing fields provide nearly all constituent concepts -
action, coupling, feedback, transition, synchronization, communication,
coordination, and situated interpretation - but no single theory
supplies a cross-domain identity, composition, and comparison framework.
The warranted contribution is therefore a minimal synthesis, not a new
primitive: a typed interaction ontology, episode lifecycle,
compositional grammar, algebraic operators, identity criteria,
invariants, interaction contract, and falsification matrix.

# 1. Problem and Method

The word interaction often performs explanatory work without identifying
what kind of phenomenon occurred. In interface research it may mean a
sequence of user inputs and system outputs. In cybernetics it can imply
feedback. In communication theory it may mean exchange of messages. In
ecological psychology it can indicate organism-environment reciprocity.
In formal computer science it can mean synchronization or communication
between processes. In social theory it may refer to jointly produced
order. These uses overlap, but none can be assumed to define the others.

The analysis used a cross-disciplinary boundary method. For each
tradition, the study identified: (1) the entities allowed to interact;
(2) the relation or mechanism linking them; (3) whether reciprocity,
intention, communication, observation, or state change is required; (4)
the temporal unit; (5) the evidence by which interaction is established;
and (6) the formal resources available for identity and composition.
Candidate definitions were then tested against counterexamples including
passive sensing, unilateral control, delayed feedback, hidden API
effects, failed communication, and simultaneous but independent
activity.

The supplied corpus was used as foundational evidence for ecological,
situated, distributed, activity-theoretic, cognitive-engineering, and
interaction-design perspectives. The methodological standard followed
the Research Canon: concepts were retained only when necessary,
definitions were separated from implementations, and major claims were
made falsifiable and operationalizable.

# 2. Existing Conceptions of Interaction

No accepted universal definition exists. The major traditions organize
interaction around different explanatory targets.

Ecological psychology treats organism and environment as complementary
rather than independent explanatory domains. Gibson\'s affordances are
possibilities of action relative to an animal-environment system. This
supplies relationality but does not by itself define an interaction
episode, identity, or composition.

Cybernetics organizes control and communication through feedback. Wiener
placed messages and responses within circular regulation. Feedback gives
a strong mechanism for recurrent interaction, but open-loop influence
and one-shot synchronized events show that feedback is not necessary for
every interaction token.

Systems theory commonly treats interaction as mutual influence among
components whose collective behavior is not recoverable from isolated
components alone. This supplies dependence and emergence but often
leaves interaction boundaries and empirical identity underspecified.

Situated action and ethnomethodological approaches reject the view that
plans fully determine conduct. Suchman describes successful interaction
as collaboratively produced intelligibility responsive to contingencies
and others\' actions. This supplies situated accomplishment and
interpretive coordination, but it is too restrictive for non-semantic
physical and computational interactions.

Distributed cognition locates cognitive organization across people,
artifacts, and representational media. Hutchins shows that coordinated
transformations across a system can constitute the relevant cognitive
process. This supports system-level interaction and mediation but makes
boundaries a substantive modeling decision.

Activity theory places action within object-oriented, tool-mediated,
socially organized activity. It captures historical and institutional
mediation, yet its unit is often too large for atomic computational
interaction.

HCI contains multiple theories rather than one definition. Cognitive
engineering models user-system exchanges quantitatively; embodied
interaction treats meaning as arising through engaged practice;
instrumental and generative theories organize design around action and
adaptation; computational rationality explains interaction as adaptation
under bounds. These theories explain important classes of interaction
but are not extensionally equivalent.

Communication theory distinguishes transmission from meaning. Shannon\'s
mathematical theory explains signal selection and uncertainty without
requiring semantic understanding. Speech-act and agent-communication
theories add illocutionary force and protocol commitments. Communication
is therefore one interaction mechanism, not interaction\'s genus.

Control theory defines systems through inputs, states, outputs, and
dynamical response. Coupling occurs when one subsystem\'s output enters
another\'s dynamics. This gives precise counterfactual and temporal
machinery, but interaction cannot be reduced to successful control
because uncontrolled perturbation and negotiation also qualify.

Formal methods represent interaction through synchronization, shared
events, message passing, handshakes, shared variables, or transitions.
CCS, CSP, process algebras, labeled transition systems, event
structures, and protocol models provide composition and behavioral
equivalence. Their strength is formal precision; their limitation is
that semantic and social interpretation normally lies outside the
transition semantics.

Robotics and multi-agent systems treat interaction through sensing,
action, communication, coordination, negotiation, and joint task
execution. Protocols specify admissible message sequences and roles.
These approaches show that interaction may be globally specified but
locally enacted, and that composition can fail when local agents cannot
realize a global protocol.

Philosophy of action distinguishes intentional action from mere movement
or event. This blocks a definition of interaction as simply two actions:
many interactions include non-agentive components, unintended
consequences, or automatic responses.

# 3. Reductive Tests

Interaction cannot be reduced to action. An action can occur without
another system being coupled to it, while an interaction can include
passive dynamics, automatic responses, or non-intentional perturbations.
Action is attributable to an agent under some theory of agency;
interaction concerns dependence among processes.

Interaction cannot be reduced to behavior. Behavior is an observed or
modeled pattern attributable to a system. Two systems can behave
simultaneously without interacting, and a system\'s behavior may be
evidence of interaction without constituting the relation itself.

Interaction cannot be reduced to communication. Mechanical contact,
resource contention, sensorimotor coupling, and shared-state
interference can be interactions without messages or shared meaning.
Conversely, a transmitted message that produces no uptake may constitute
attempted communication but may fail to establish an interaction episode
under a causal-dependence criterion.

Interaction cannot be reduced to computation. Computation can occur
internally without coupling to another system. Some interactions are
physical, biological, or social and are not usefully described as
computation. Computational interaction is one domain-specific
realization.

Interaction cannot be reduced to observation. Observation may be
unilateral and non-perturbative at the modeled scale. It becomes
interaction when sensing changes subsequent trajectories, when
measurement perturbs the observed system, or when observation
participates in a recurrent loop.

Interaction cannot be reduced to a state transition. A state transition
can be internal and autonomous. Interaction requires that at least part
of a transition\'s occurrence, probability, timing, or reachable
consequences depend on another distinguishable system through a
coupling.

Interaction cannot be reduced to causation in general. A falling rock
may cause a mark in soil, but a single one-way causal event does not
automatically justify an interaction episode. The term is most useful
when the coupling creates reciprocal or recurrent constraint across the
participants\' trajectories. Reciprocity need not be equal or immediate;
it may be mediated through a shared environment and realized over time.

These failures do not establish interaction as metaphysically primitive.
They establish it as a non-redundant analytical relation composed from
existing notions of system, state, process, coupling, perturbation,
constraint, and temporal dependence.

# 4. Canonical Definition

Interaction episode: a bounded interval in which two or more
distinguishable systems are coupled such that perturbations originating
in, or mediated by, one system alter the possible or actual state
trajectory of at least one other system, and the resulting configuration
constrains a later trajectory of an originating or co-participating
system.

This definition has six commitments.

First, interaction is relational. It is not located exclusively in
either participant.

Second, interaction is processual. It is extended over at least an
analytically distinguishable sequence, even when implemented as an
apparently atomic synchronization.

Third, interaction requires coupling. A pathway must exist through which
perturbation, constraint, resource competition, synchronization, signal,
or material effect can pass.

Fourth, interaction requires counterfactual dependence. Holding relevant
background conditions fixed, removing or changing the coupling or
participant would change some participant\'s reachable, probable, timed,
or actual trajectory.

Fifth, interaction requires reciprocal closure at the episode level. The
reciprocal effect can be direct, indirect, asymmetric, delayed,
probabilistic, or environmentally mediated. A single isolated one-way
influence is causation but not yet interaction under the strict
definition.

Sixth, every interaction claim is boundary- and timescale-relative. What
appears unilateral over milliseconds may be reciprocal over seconds;
what appears dyadic may be mediated by infrastructure, institutions, or
environments when the boundary expands.

# 5. Necessary and Non-Necessary Conditions

Necessary conditions are: distinguishable participants or subsystems; a
coupling relation; at least one transmitted perturbation or constraint;
counterfactual effect on a participant trajectory; reciprocal or
recurrent closure within the declared episode; and explicit boundary and
timescale.

Not necessary are: biological agency; conscious intention; semantic
content; successful communication; mutual awareness; equality of
influence; simultaneous response; visible interface events; goal
agreement; positive outcome; or permanent state change.

Observable state change is not strictly necessary if the interaction
changes transition probabilities, timing, control margins, uncertainty,
or reachable possibilities without producing an immediately observed
macrostate change. Such claims require stronger evidence than direct
transition traces.

Interaction may fail. A protocol can deadlock, a conversational repair
can collapse, or a control loop can oscillate. Failure does not erase
the interaction; it changes its outcome and lifecycle state.

# 6. Interaction Ontology

The minimal ontology contains established constructs rather than newly
coined entities.

Participant: a system or subsystem treated as distinguishable for the
analysis.

State: the variables considered sufficient to characterize a participant
at a time and scale.

Process: an ordered or partially ordered evolution of state.

Boundary: the inclusion rule separating participants, environment, and
background conditions.

Coupling: a relation through which one participant or shared medium can
affect another participant\'s transition structure.

Perturbation: a difference propagated through a coupling relation.

Constraint: a change in possible, probable, timed, or admissible
trajectories.

Uptake: incorporation of a perturbation into a participant transition or
control process. Uptake need not be semantic.

Response: a subsequent transition attributable partly to uptake.

Recurrence: return influence through which a response constrains an
earlier source, co-participant, or shared coupling configuration.

Episode: a bounded segment containing initiation, coupling, uptake,
response, and sufficient closure for identity.

Trace: a temporally ordered or partially ordered record of observable
events and state estimates.

Protocol: a rule system constraining admissible interaction traces.

Outcome: the episode-relative resulting state, distribution, commitment,
or termination condition.

Context: background conditions that affect coupling or interpretation
but are not modeled as participants in the focal episode.

Environment: modeled external dynamics through which participants may be
coupled.

Invariant: a declared property preserved across an interaction,
representation, implementation, or decomposition.

# 7. Interaction Primitives and Grammar

The theory does not claim metaphysical primitives. It proposes
analytical primitives sufficient for representation.

A minimal event vocabulary is:

bind(p, q, c): establish or activate coupling c between participants p
and q.\
emit(p, d): participant p produces perturbation d.\
transmit(c, d): coupling c carries d.\
uptake(q, d): d changes q\'s transition conditions or state.\
respond(q, r): q undergoes or produces response r.\
recur(r, p\|c): r constrains p or the coupling configuration.\
commit(o): an outcome or commitment becomes episode-relevant.\
fail(f): a declared failure condition occurs.\
unbind(c): coupling terminates or becomes inactive.

A minimal interaction grammar is:

Episode ::= Boundary Initiation CoupledProcess Closure\
CoupledProcess ::= Exchange \| Synchronization \| SharedMedium \|
Feedback \| Coordination\
Exchange ::= Emit Transmit Uptake \[Response\]\
Synchronization ::= JointEvent constrained-by Participants\
SharedMedium ::= ParticipantEffect MediumTransition ParticipantUptake\
Feedback ::= Exchange Recurrence+\
Coordination ::= CoupledProcess constrained-by Protocol\
Closure ::= Recurrence \| JointCommitment \| StableTermination \|
DeclaredTimeout \| Failure

The grammar separates implementation form from interaction identity. A
message exchange, button press, physical collision, or shared-memory
write may instantiate the same abstract roles while differing in
semantics and mechanism.

# 8. Interaction Lifecycle

1\. Eligibility: participants, capacities, permissions, and
preconditions make coupling possible.\
2. Initiation: a participant or environmental condition activates a
coupling pathway.\
3. Perturbation: a difference is produced and propagated.\
4. Uptake: another participant\'s state or transition structure becomes
dependent on that difference.\
5. Response: a consequential transition occurs.\
6. Recurrence or closure: the response returns influence, establishes a
joint commitment, reaches stable termination, times out, or fails.\
7. Aftereffect: participant states, beliefs, policies, coupling
strength, or future opportunities may change.

These phases are analytical, not universally sequential. Synchronization
can merge initiation, uptake, and response. Distributed interaction can
contain concurrent branches. Repeated interaction can overlap
aftereffects with the eligibility conditions of later episodes.

# 9. Identity and Invariants

Interaction identity is not exhausted by event equality. The same
interaction may be rendered through different modalities,
implementations, or trace granularities. Conversely, superficially
identical event sequences may constitute different interactions when
participants, semantics, authority, or causal dependencies differ.

An interaction identity claim must declare: participants and roles;
focal boundary; timescale; coupling topology; relevant state variables;
protocol or admissibility conditions; causal or counterfactual
dependencies; initiation and closure criteria; and invariants.

Strong token identity requires continuity of the same causal episode.
Type identity requires equivalence under a declared abstraction.

Candidate invariants include:

Participant-role invariance: the same abstract roles are preserved
despite implementation changes.\
Protocol invariance: admissible ordering and obligation structure are
preserved.\
Transition invariance: corresponding actions induce equivalent abstract
state changes.\
Causal-structure invariance: the counterfactual dependency graph is
preserved.\
Outcome invariance: declared terminal conditions or distributions are
preserved.\
Information invariance: selected distinctions available to participants
are preserved.\
Opportunity invariance: relevant feasible, permitted, exposed, and
recoverable actions are preserved.\
Behavioral invariance: trace distributions remain equivalent under a
metric and tolerance.

No invariant is universal. Every equivalence claim must name the
preserved relation, observer, abstraction, context, and tolerance.

# 10. Interaction Algebra

Let an interaction type I be represented as a tuple:

I = \<P, S, C, E, T, R, B, K\>

where P is a set of participants and roles; S is a structured state
space; C is a coupling topology; E is a typed event set; T is a
transition or stochastic kernel; R is a recurrence and dependency
relation; B specifies boundary and timescale; and K specifies closure
conditions and invariants.

The following operators are sufficient for a minimal compositional
algebra.

Sequential composition I ; J: J begins after a closure condition of I
and may inherit a mapped state.

Parallel composition I \|\| J: episodes proceed concurrently with
independent or shared participants.

Synchronization I sync_A J: episodes must jointly participate in events
from synchronization set A.

Choice I + J: one of several admissible episode structures is realized.

Iteration I\*: zero or more recurrent instances under a termination
rule.

Mediation M\[I\]: interaction I is realized through mediator or
environment M.

Restriction I\\H: selected events or coupling channels are hidden from
an observer while remaining causally active.

Abstraction alpha(I): implementation events are mapped to a coarser
interaction type.

Refinement I \<= J: J preserves the declared invariants and allowed
behavior of I while adding implementation detail.

Interference I bowtie J: concurrent interactions share state or
resources such that each changes the other\'s reachable traces.

These operators borrow from process algebra, transition systems, and
systems theory. The proposed synthesis adds explicit participant roles,
episode boundaries, recurrence criteria, and cross-domain invariants.
Algebraic laws are conditional rather than universal. Sequential
composition is not necessarily commutative; parallel composition may
cease to be associative when resource or timing assumptions change;
abstraction must preserve declared observables to support equivalence.

# 11. Composition Rules

Interactions compose only when boundary mappings are valid. A
participant in one episode may become an environment, mediator, or
internal subsystem in another abstraction.

State compatibility: the terminal state distribution of the first
episode must satisfy the initial-state assumptions of the second.

Role compatibility: inherited participant roles and authority must
remain meaningful.

Coupling compatibility: channels, shared variables, or physical
interfaces must connect without introducing unmodeled transformations.

Temporal compatibility: ordering, concurrency, deadlines, and latency
assumptions must be satisfiable.

Semantic compatibility: where messages or commitments are involved,
content interpretations and protocol meanings must align.

Invariant compatibility: composition must not silently violate safety,
identity, or observational equivalence conditions.

Closure discipline: a subinteraction may be incomplete while the
containing interaction remains active, but its completion, timeout,
cancellation, or compensation must be represented.

Composition is therefore not mere concatenation of event logs. It is a
constrained construction over state, roles, coupling, time, and
invariants.

# 12. Comparative Cases

Human-human conversation. Participants alternate and overlap utterances,
gestures, gaze, repair, and inference. Communication and semantic
interpretation are central, but the interaction also includes timing,
turn allocation, mutual orientation, and embodied feedback. Identity
depends on the evolving joint episode rather than isolated messages.

Human-computer interaction. A user action changes system state or
presented information; the resulting projection changes the user\'s
opportunities, beliefs, or next action. Reciprocity is asymmetric
because the computational system need not possess intention. Interaction
is established by coupled trajectories, not by anthropomorphic agency.

Agent-agent interaction. Agents exchange messages, synchronize on shared
state, negotiate, or coordinate through protocols. Interaction can be
formally represented as global protocols and local enactments. Failed
enactability demonstrates that a global trace specification is not
sufficient unless local participants can realize it.

API interaction. A client request invokes a service transition, and the
response, error, side effect, or timeout changes the client\'s later
state or policy. A fire-and-forget request with no later client
dependence may be a unilateral invocation; an episode becomes
interaction when returned or shared-state effects constrain subsequent
behavior.

Physical interaction. Two bodies collide, deform, transfer momentum, and
alter each other\'s trajectories. There is no required communication or
interpretation. Reciprocal physical dependence provides the clearest
minimal example.

Conversational interaction with a computational agent. Messages are
represented as linguistic acts, but the underlying episode also includes
model state, tool availability, authorization, latency, and projection.
Apparent semantic reciprocity can exceed actual computational
capability, so interaction analysis must separate signaled, believed,
and feasible transitions.

Across all six cases, what remains common is not intention, language,
interface, or computation. It is bounded reciprocal constraint through
coupling, observable or inferable in participant trajectories.

# 13. Evidence and Operationalization

Direct evidence includes synchronized event traces, state measurements,
messages, control signals, resource changes, and observed transitions.
Derived evidence includes reconstructed causal graphs, reachability
differences, transfer functions, protocol conformance, and temporal
dependencies. Interpretive evidence includes inferred intention,
meaning, belief, coordination, and social significance.

A minimal empirical test for interaction compares a coupled condition
with a suitably matched decoupled or perturbed condition. Evidence
should show that changing participant A or coupling C changes B\'s
trajectory and that B\'s resulting state or response changes a later
trajectory of A, C, or a shared system within the episode boundary.

Possible measures include conditional mutual information, intervention
effects, transfer entropy, Granger-style temporal dependence, impulse
response, synchronization, cross-recurrence, state-transition
divergence, protocol trace conformance, and causal model comparison.
None alone proves interaction. Statistical dependence without a
plausible coupling may be confounding; causal influence without
recurrence may be unilateral causation; synchronized traces may share an
external driver.

For semantic and social interaction, additional evidence may include
repair sequences, uptake displays, commitment changes, alignment, or
coordinated task transitions. Such evidence should not be generalized to
physical or non-semantic interaction.

# 14. Falsification Tests

The theory should be rejected or narrowed if any of the following is
demonstrated.

Reduction to transition systems: if standard transition-system semantics
can represent participants, coupling, recurrence, episode identity,
interpretation boundaries, and cross-domain composition without
additional commitments, the proposed ontology adds no explanatory value.

Reciprocity failure: if scientific practice consistently classifies
one-way causal influence as interaction and no explanatory or predictive
gain follows from distinguishing it, reciprocal closure should be
removed from the definition.

Boundary non-reproducibility: if independent researchers cannot agree on
episode boundaries and timescales under explicit rules, interaction
identity may be too observer-relative for stable comparison.

Counterfactual non-identifiability: if coupled and merely correlated
trajectories cannot be distinguished even in principle for relevant
domains, interaction cannot support causal explanation there.

Composition failure: if the algebra cannot predict or explain properties
of composed episodes beyond raw event concatenation, it should be
treated as notation rather than theory.

Invariant failure: if no useful property can be preserved across
implementation-independent representations of interaction, claims of
general interaction types should be abandoned.

Existing-theory sufficiency: if one established theory provides
equivalent vocabulary, ontology, mechanisms, formalization, and
empirical predictions across all comparative cases, the synthesis should
be replaced by that theory.

Predictive null: if interaction-level variables do not improve
explanation or prediction over participant-level states, independent
causal models, and background context, interaction may be merely
descriptive.

# 15. Threats to Validity

The definition privileges reciprocal constraint and may exclude ordinary
language uses such as a person interacting once with a passive artifact.
This is deliberate but contestable. The stricter definition seeks
explanatory discrimination; broader usage may be appropriate in design
practice.

Counterfactual dependence is model-relative. Incorrect state variables,
hidden common causes, or poorly chosen timescales can create or erase
apparent interaction. Reciprocal effects may be too weak or delayed to
estimate.

The framework combines traditions with incompatible ontological
assumptions. Ecological psychology resists internal representational
explanations; formal computer science abstracts away material
embodiment; social theory treats meaning and accountability as locally
accomplished. The synthesis claims a shared structural layer, not
theoretical unification of all explanatory levels.

Formal composition can obscure situated transformation. Real
participants reinterpret protocols, change goals, and alter boundaries.
Interaction types should therefore be treated as models with scope
conditions, not exhaustive descriptions.

The comparative cases are selected to maximize diversity, but they do
not establish universality. Biological symbiosis, market interaction,
quantum interaction, and institutional interaction may require
revisions.

# 16. Conclusion

Interaction is not a primitive substance, action type, or universal
mechanism. Nor is it adequately reducible to action, behavior,
communication, computation, observation, state transition, feedback, or
causation alone.

The literature supports a minimal cross-disciplinary synthesis:
interaction is a bounded, temporally organized relation of reciprocal
constraint among distinguishable systems through coupling. Its tokens
are established by counterfactual dependence in participant
trajectories; its types are defined only under declared boundaries,
roles, abstractions, and invariants. Communication, synchronization,
feedback, coordination, collision, shared-state interference, and
situated meaning-making are mechanisms or forms of interaction rather
than synonyms.

Existing disciplines provide the constituent theory, but no single one
provides a complete cross-domain account of identity, composition,
invariance, and evidence. The minimum conceptual addition is therefore
not a new primitive. It is a shared interaction contract and typed
compositional framework that makes existing concepts interoperable and
empirically testable.

## Dependency Graph

Ontology -\> state and participant identity -\> coupling -\> opportunity
-\> perturbation and uptake -\> interaction episode -\> interpretation
and policy -\> behavior -\> evidence and measurement -\> comparison and
prediction.

## Interaction Comparison Protocol

1\. Declare the focal boundary, timescale, participants, roles, and
state abstraction.

2\. Identify coupling mechanisms and construct a counterfactual
decoupled baseline.

3\. Enumerate observable events, hidden state assumptions, and
uncertainty.

4\. Test directed influence and reciprocal or recurrent closure.

5\. Identify protocol, semantic, causal, outcome, opportunity, and
behavioral invariants separately.

6\. Compare traces only after aligning state abstraction and event
granularity.

7\. Control for common causes, shared external drivers, latency, and
measurement artifacts.

8\. State whether the claim concerns token identity, type equivalence,
refinement, or similarity.

9\. Report failures, deadlocks, timeouts, and recovery as part of the
interaction rather than deleting them.

10\. Declare the conditions under which the comparison would be
falsified.

**Behavior**

*Toward a Scientific Theory of Computational Behavior*

Cross-disciplinary foundational research paper

# Abstract

Behavior is indispensable across psychology, ethology, cognitive
science, economics, reinforcement learning, cybernetics, robotics,
systems theory, human-computer interaction, and philosophy of action,
yet the term refers variously to movement, response, output, action,
policy, performance, conduct, and organism-environment coordination.
This paper asks what constitutes behavior and how it should be
represented scientifically without dependence on a particular interface
or technology.

The review finds no single accepted definition, but it identifies a
stable analytical core. Behavior is best treated as a bounded,
temporally extended trajectory of observable or instrumentally
recoverable changes attributable to a system in relation to its
environment. Behavior is not identical to state, because it concerns
change or persistence across time; not identical to action, because
action normally adds agency, organization, or purposive interpretation;
not identical to interaction, because interaction requires reciprocal
constraint between distinguishable systems; and not identical to a
policy, strategy, intention, or goal, which are explanatory or latent
structures rather than observations.

Existing theories are sufficient for most component problems but lack a
shared evidence-preserving representation spanning human, animal, and
artificial systems. The paper therefore proposes a typed trace framework
rather than a new behavioral primitive. It separates raw records,
detected events, attributed behavioral events, episodes, patterns,
actions, strategies, and latent explanations. It supplies a behavior
ontology, behavioral grammar, trace model, evidence hierarchy, taxonomy,
annotation contract, and falsification criteria. Its central claim is
that scientifically useful behavioral representation requires explicit
system boundaries, observation functions, temporal segmentation rules,
attribution criteria, context, uncertainty, and a prohibition against
treating latent explanations as direct observations.

# 1. Problem and Scope

Computational interaction research frequently treats clicks, commands,
gaze shifts, messages, state changes, task completion, and model outputs
as behavior. These records are not equivalent. Some are environmental
measurements, some are system transitions, some are experimenter-defined
events, and some are interpretations of agency, purpose, belief, or
strategy. Without a theory of behavior, interaction traces risk becoming
collections of implementation-specific events whose explanatory status
is unclear.

The problem is not solved by defining behavior as whatever a system
does. That formulation is too broad to distinguish behavior from
internal dynamics, passive displacement, noise, or arbitrary state
change. Conversely, limiting behavior to intentional human action
excludes organisms, robots, adaptive software, reflexes, omissions, and
learned but non-deliberative conduct. A useful account must remain
implementation-independent while retaining empirical discipline.

The paper evaluates whether established theories already supply a
sufficient account. The objective is not a universal metaphysical
definition. It is a minimal scientific architecture adequate for
representing behavioral evidence across computational interactions.

# 2. Method and Standards

The review compares explanatory structures rather than recounting
disciplinary histories. Primary and foundational works were prioritized:
Dewey on the reflex arc; Skinner on operant behavior; Tinbergen on
ethological explanation; Rosenblueth, Wiener, and Bigelow on behavioral
classification and purpose; Ryle and philosophy of action on
dispositions and agency; Newell and Simon on problem-solving protocols;
ecological and situated approaches on organism-environment coordination;
reinforcement learning on policies and trajectories; and HCI on task
performance, action sequences, and interaction logs.

For each tradition, the analysis identifies: the entity to which
behavior is attributed; the temporal unit; the role of environment;
whether purpose or intention is required; the observational basis; the
explanatory mechanism; and the treatment of latent variables. Candidate
distinctions are retained only when counterexamples show that collapsing
them would generate false inferences. This follows the project\'s canon:
define vocabulary, separate observation from interpretation, prefer
mechanisms, require operationalization and falsifiability, and leave
reusable artifacts.

# 4. Canonical Distinctions

## 4.1 State, change, and behavior

A state is a description of a system at a time or over an interval.
Behavior concerns a trajectory, transition pattern, controlled
persistence, or temporally organized relation among states. Remaining
still can count as behavior when maintaining position is attributable to
regulation or policy; mere static existence does not. This means change
is not strictly necessary, but temporal organization and counterfactual
sensitivity are.

Internal state change is not automatically behavior. A memory
allocation, hidden neural activation, or background process becomes
behavioral evidence only relative to a declared observational level and
attribution rule. Otherwise every physical change inside a system would
count, eliminating useful boundaries.

## 4.2 Behavior and action

Behavior is the broader evidential category. Action adds an attribution
of agency, organization, control, or purposive relevance. A reflex,
drift, involuntary movement, policy output, and failed attempt can be
behavioral without satisfying a demanding theory of action. Conversely,
an omission may qualify as action when an agent could and was expected
to intervene, even though no overt movement occurred. Action is
therefore not reducible to a visible event.

The framework treats action attribution as typed and defeasible.
Researchers must specify whether an event is merely attributed to a
system, controlled by it, selected by a policy, intended, reason-guided,
or normatively accountable.

## 4.3 Behavior and interaction

Behavior can be attributed to one system relative to an environment.
Interaction requires reciprocal constraint between distinguishable
systems. An agent\'s behavior may occur within an interaction, but not
every behavior is interactive, and an interaction trace contains events
attributable to multiple participants and mediating structures. Behavior
is therefore a component and perspective on interaction, not its
synonym.

## 4.4 Behavior and performance

Performance evaluates behavior against a task, norm, utility, or success
criterion. The same behavioral trajectory can be high-performing under
one objective and poor under another. Completion, reward, speed,
accuracy, and efficiency are evaluative functions over behavior; they
are not behavior itself.

## 4.5 Behavior and latent explanation

Intention, belief, preference, confidence, strategy, habit, expertise,
attention, workload, and policy are not directly observed in ordinary
traces. They are latent or theoretical variables inferred from behavior,
reports, interventions, and auxiliary measurements. A scientific
representation must preserve this evidential asymmetry. An action log
can constrain interpretations but rarely identifies one uniquely.

# 5. Canonical Definition

Behavior is a bounded, temporally extended trajectory of observable or
instrumentally recoverable changes, outputs, or regulated persistence
attributable to a system in relation to its environment under a declared
observation model.

Each clause is necessary for scientific use:

Bounded: the behaving system and relevant environment must be
specified.\
Temporally extended: behavior is identified through ordering, duration,
transition, recurrence, or maintained regulation.\
Observable or recoverable: evidence must be accessible through declared
instruments or records.\
Attributable: the trajectory must be assigned to a system by an explicit
causal, control, ownership, or analytic rule.\
Relational: behavior is interpreted relative to environmental conditions
and opportunities.\
Observation-model relative: event types, granularity, and uncertainty
depend on how the phenomenon is measured.

This definition does not require consciousness, intention, semantic
understanding, optimality, success, movement, or direct observation by a
human. It also does not claim that behavior exists only when observed.
Rather, scientific claims about behavior require an observation model
connecting the target process to evidence.

# 6. Behavioral Event and Segmentation

A behavioral event is not a self-identifying atom. It is a temporally
bounded segment of a trace classified under an event type and attributed
to a system. Segmentation may be physical, functional, task-relative,
protocol-defined, or statistically inferred. Different segmentations can
be valid for different explanatory questions.

The smallest useful unit is therefore not universally a click, movement,
command, or state transition. It is the minimal discriminable segment
required by a declared explanatory and measurement contract. For motor
control this may be a subsecond trajectory; for HCI it may be an
operation; for organizational activity it may be a coordinated episode;
for reinforcement learning it may be a time step; for discourse it may
be a turn or act. Units must not be compared across studies without
declaring their segmentation rules.

# 8. Behavioral Grammar

A behavioral grammar specifies admissible composition without claiming
that behavior is linguistic. The minimum grammar distinguishes records,
events, episodes, and explanatory annotations.

Record r ::= \<source, time, channel, value, provenance, uncertainty\>\
Event e ::= detect(type, interval, records, rule)\
Attributed event b ::= attribute(system, event, relation, confidence)\
Episode q ::= compose(boundary, order, {b}, context, completion)\
Trace τ ::= partial-order({records, events, episodes}, clocks,
missingness)\
Interpretation i ::= infer(construct, evidence-set, model, alternatives,
uncertainty)\
Outcome o ::= evaluate(trace-or-episode, criterion, tolerance)

Composition operators include sequential composition (;), concurrency
(\|\|), choice (+), iteration (\*), interruption (!), omission (Ø under
an expectation model), and nesting (\[ \]). These operators describe
trace organization. They do not imply purpose or meaning by themselves.

# 9. Trace Model

A scientific trace should be modeled as more than an ordered list.
Distributed and asynchronous systems require partial ordering, multiple
clocks, uncertain timestamps, concurrent events, hidden state, and
provenance.

Let a behavioral trace be:

τ = \<R, E, A, Q, ≺, C, Ω\>

R is the set of raw records. E is the set of detected events. A maps
events to attributed systems and relation types. Q is a set of episodes
or higher-order segmentations. ≺ is a temporal or causal partial order.
C is context, including task, opportunity profile, projection,
permissions, environment, and prior history. Ω records uncertainty,
missingness, detector error, attribution confidence, and competing
annotations.

A trace is evidence, not a complete account of behavior. What was not
instrumented may be absent. Identical traces may arise from different
mechanisms; different traces may instantiate the same strategy or task
outcome. Trace equivalence must therefore be typed by observables,
granularity, context, and tolerance.

# 12. Cross-System Comparative Cases

Human-computer command. A user invokes a command, the system logs an
event, and a state transition follows. The record supports that an input
occurred and may support attribution to the account or device. It does
not alone establish intention, understanding, confidence, or authorship
by the human rather than automation.

Animal navigation. A trajectory through an environment is directly
behavioral under an organism boundary. Explaining it as foraging,
homing, or exploration requires environmental and functional evidence.
Tinbergen\'s distinctions show that mechanism, development, adaptive
function, and phylogeny answer different questions about the same
behavior.

Robot obstacle avoidance. Sensor, control, and motion traces support a
mechanistic account. Goal-directedness can be specified functionally
without assuming consciousness. The behavior may be generated by
feedback control, a learned policy, or a fixed rule; output similarity
does not identify the mechanism.

Reinforcement-learning agent. A state-action-reward trajectory is
behavior under the model, while the policy is a generative disposition
over actions. The environment\'s state representation is analytical, not
necessarily the system\'s own representation. Reward is an evaluative
signal, not evidence of subjective desire.

Distributed team activity. The relevant behavior may not be attributable
to any individual. Coordination emerges across people, artifacts, and
representations. A group-level episode requires explicit composition and
boundary rules, preserving individual and collective levels rather than
replacing one with the other.

Conversational system. Generated text is observable output. Treating it
as assertion, promise, refusal, deception, or understanding requires
semantic, institutional, and agency criteria. Surface linguistic form is
insufficient to establish the latent construct.

# 13. Recurring Behavioral Structures

-   Feedback loops: outputs alter conditions that shape later behavior.

-   Selection under constraints: behavior is chosen or generated from an
    opportunity structure, whether explicitly represented or not.

-   Temporal hierarchy: events compose into episodes, routines,
    strategies, and developmental trajectories.

-   Partial observability: the behaving system and observer have
    incomplete and different access to state.

-   Adaptation: response distributions change with history,
    consequences, training, and environmental structure.

-   Equifinality and multifinality: different mechanisms can produce
    similar traces, and similar initial traces can lead to different
    outcomes.

-   Context sensitivity: task, environment, social rules, projection,
    and prior activity alter the meaning of identical events.

-   Coordination: behavior may be jointly organized across agents and
    artifacts.

-   Error and recovery: failed or interrupted action changes subsequent
    behavior and opportunity.

-   Persistence and omission: maintaining a state or not acting can be
    behavior under control or expectation models.

# 14. Latent Variables

Latent variables are legitimate when they support testable measurement
models, interventions, or predictions. They become scientifically
dangerous when labels merely redescribe the behavior they are supposed
to explain. Saying that a user clicked because of a preference, inferred
only from the click, is circular unless preference independently
predicts behavior across conditions.

A latent claim should declare: construct definition; indicators;
measurement model; temporal ordering; alternative explanations;
identification assumptions; expected interventions; uncertainty; and
falsifying observations. Self-report is additional behavior and
evidence, not transparent access to an internal state. Model-generated
hidden states are computational variables, not automatically
psychological constructs.

The recommended policy is typed inference. Terms such as intended,
believed, understood, attended, preferred, confused, and strategic must
be explicitly marked as reported, experimentally manipulated,
model-inferred, or theoretically attributed.

# 17. Threats to Validity

The proposed definition is intentionally scientific rather than
exhaustive of ordinary language. It may classify phenomena differently
from legal, moral, clinical, or folk-psychological accounts. The term
attributable risks importing causal assumptions into description; this
is mitigated by requiring attribution types and uncertainty.

The framework may privilege traceable computational cases. Human and
animal behavior can involve embodied, affective, social, historical, and
institutional structures not recoverable from event logs. Distributed
cognition also makes system boundaries contested rather than simply
discoverable.

Formal traces can encourage false completeness. Missing channels,
observer effects, coding choices, and asynchronous processes may
materially alter conclusions. Behavioral categories can become reified,
particularly when inferred properties are attached to demographic
groups. Culture, language, occupation, disability, and experience should
enter through measured contexts and mechanisms rather than deterministic
labels.

Finally, the framework\'s value is unproven until independent
researchers can annotate common datasets more consistently, compare
behavior across implementations, and improve explanatory or predictive
performance without laundering interpretation as observation.

# 18. Implications for Computational Interaction Research

The framework places behavior after interaction and opportunity but
before measurement and prediction. Interaction specifies reciprocal
coupling. Opportunity specifies typed action availability. Behavior
records the realized, attributed trajectory. Measurement establishes how
traces and constructs are operationalized. Explanation connects behavior
to mechanisms without assuming that representation directly causes
action.

A complete analysis should therefore distinguish: what the system made
possible; what was exposed or believed; what records were produced;
which events were detected; which events were attributed as behavior;
which actions or strategies were inferred; and which outcomes were
evaluated. This separation prevents common errors such as treating an
unselected control as unnoticed, a pause as confusion, task completion
as understanding, or equal outcomes as equal behavior.

The model also makes later similarity research tractable. Two
interactions may be semantically equivalent while producing different
behavioral traces; two traces may be structurally different while
instantiating the same policy; and behavior may be observationally
equivalent under one instrument but distinguishable under another.

# 19. Conclusion

Existing behavioral theories are sufficient for their established
domains but do not provide a single evidence-preserving vocabulary for
computational interaction. The missing contribution is not a new
substance called computational behavior. It is a disciplined synthesis
separating records, events, attribution, episodes, action, performance,
and latent explanation.

Behavior should be represented as a bounded, temporally extended,
observation-model-relative trajectory attributable to a system in
relation to its environment. This account supports humans, animals,
robots, software agents, and distributed systems without requiring
intention or reducing behavior to arbitrary state change. It preserves
the distinction between what occurred and why it occurred.

The paper\'s principal conclusion is therefore: existing theories are
conceptually sufficient but require a shared typed trace and evidence
framework for computational interaction research. The framework should
be retained only if it improves annotation reliability, cross-system
comparison, causal clarity, and out-of-sample explanation or prediction.

# 20. Reusable Artifacts

## 20.1 Canonical vocabulary

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Term**                            **Definition**
  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Behavior                            A bounded, temporally extended
                                      trajectory of observable or
                                      recoverable changes, outputs, or
                                      regulated persistence attributable
                                      to a system in relation to its
                                      environment under a declared
                                      observation model.

  Behavioral event                    A temporally bounded segment of a
                                      trace classified under an event
                                      type and attributed to a system.

  Action                              Behavior attributed as controlled,
                                      selected, intentional,
                                      reason-guided, or normatively
                                      attributable under a declared
                                      theory of agency.

  State                               A declared description of a system
                                      or environment at a time or
                                      interval.

  Trace                               A time-indexed or partially ordered
                                      collection of records, detected
                                      events, attributions, episodes,
                                      context, and uncertainty.

  Episode                             A bounded composition of behavioral
                                      events under explicit initiation,
                                      continuation, and completion rules.

  Pattern                             A regularity across events or
                                      episodes under a declared
                                      similarity rule.

  Performance                         Evaluation of behavior relative to
                                      a task, criterion, utility, norm,
                                      or tolerance.

  Latent construct                    An unobserved variable proposed to
                                      explain or predict evidence through
                                      a measurement or causal model.

                                      provenance, transformation,

                                      declared.
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

## 20.2 Minimal annotation schema

\<system_id, environment_id, record_id, source, timestamp_or_interval,
event_type, detector, attribution_type, attribution_confidence,
episode_id, context_id, outcome_relation, provenance, uncertainty,
alternative_annotations\>

## 20.3 Behavioral comparison protocol

-   Declare systems, environments, levels, and boundaries.

-   Align observation channels and verify instrumentation equivalence.

-   Normalize clocks, sampling, missingness, and event-detection rules.

-   Compare raw records before comparing attributed event labels.

-   Declare segmentation granularity and episode boundary rules.

-   Separate descriptive trace metrics from task-performance metrics.

-   Compare latent constructs only through equivalent measurement
    models.

-   Control opportunity, projection, task, permission, and prior
    experience.

-   Use typed equivalence claims with metrics and tolerances.

-   Report alternative annotations and uncertainty.

<!-- docs/02_Research_Papers/09_Measurement/Measurement_Toward_a_Scientific_Framework_for_Interaction_Research.md -->

**Measurement**

*Toward a Scientific Framework for Interaction Research*

Foundational research paper

# Abstract

Computational interaction research measures events, traces, task
outcomes, subjective reports, system states, and inferred constructs
such as discoverability, confidence, workload, belief, strategy, and
opportunity. These are often treated as if they belonged to a single
evidential category. They do not. Measurement theory distinguishes an
empirical relational structure from its numerical representation;
psychometrics distinguishes observed responses from latent constructs
and requires validity evidence for score interpretation; metrology
requires an explicit measurand and uncertainty statement; experimental
psychology distinguishes manipulation, observation, and inference; HCI
evaluation makes performance context-dependent; and systems engineering
emphasizes traceability from requirements to evidence.

This paper concludes that existing measurement theories are sufficient
in principle, but computational interaction research requires a shared
measurement architecture that integrates them. The proposed architecture
defines a measurement claim as a contract among a declared construct,
unit and level of analysis, observation model, instrument, coding or
transformation rule, numerical scale, uncertainty model, validity
argument, and admissible interpretation. It separates direct
observations, derived variables, model-based estimates, and latent
inferences; forbids interpreting logging precision as construct
validity; and requires comparison claims to declare invariance, context,
population, task, projection, and tolerance conditions. The paper
supplies a measurement ontology, canonical metrics, evidence taxonomy,
experimental framework, construct cards, uncertainty budgets,
comparability tests, and falsification criteria.

# 1. Problem Statement

Interaction research routinely reports time, success, error, clicks,
paths, ratings, physiological signals, and model predictions. The
apparent precision of these quantities can obscure a prior question:
what exactly has been measured? A timestamp is directly recorded;
hesitation is inferred. A control was displayed; discoverability was not
thereby measured. An action was executed; intention, understanding,
confidence, or strategy were not directly observed. A task was
completed; equal access, equal opportunity, and equivalent interaction
were not established.

The central problem is therefore not a shortage of metrics. It is the
absence of a common framework that connects theoretical constructs to
observations without collapsing observation, transformation, inference,
and interpretation. Computational interaction research requires a
measurement theory that is implementation-independent, explicit about
uncertainty, and compatible with system variables, behavioral traces,
subjective reports, and latent constructs.

# 2. Literature Review Method

The review used a concept-centered synthesis across measurement theory,
psychometrics, metrology, statistics, experimental psychology, HCI
evaluation, human factors, information theory, and systems engineering.
Foundational and primary sources were prioritized: representational
measurement theory for numerical representation and scale admissibility;
Cronbach and Meehl for construct validity; Messick for validity as an
argument about score meaning and use; the Guide to the Expression of
Uncertainty in Measurement and NIST guidance for measurands and
uncertainty; ISO 9241-11 for context-dependent usability; classical
reliability and generalizability theory; signal detection theory; causal
inference; and established HCI measures.

The synthesis was constrained by four tests. First, no new construct was
retained when an established measurement concept already sufficed.
Second, every proposed measurement category had to support
operationalization and falsification. Third, direct observations were
separated from derived and latent quantities. Fourth, comparison claims
were required to state the transformations and scope under which scores
remain interpretable.

# 3. What Measurement Is

Measurement is not merely assigning a number. In representational
measurement theory, numerical assignments are justified when the
numerical structure preserves relevant relations in an empirical
structure, and the permissible transformations of the scale determine
which comparisons and statistics remain meaningful. This yields two
central requirements: representation and uniqueness. A measure must
preserve declared empirical relations, and its interpretation must
respect the scale transformations under which that representation
remains valid.

Metrology adds the measurand: the quantity intended to be measured. A
result is incomplete without specification of the measurand, method,
conditions, and uncertainty. Psychometrics adds a further constraint:
many interaction constructs are not directly observable. Scores are
evidence-bearing observations whose interpretation as measures of a
construct requires a nomological and empirical argument.

For computational interaction, measurement is therefore defined as:

A rule-governed process that maps observations of a declared interaction
phenomenon into a representational structure, together with an
uncertainty statement and a validity argument specifying which
interpretations and comparisons are warranted.

This definition distinguishes measurement from logging, counting,
classification, estimation, and explanation. Logs may supply
observations. Counts may summarize observations. Classifiers may derive
labels. Models may estimate latent variables. None of these alone
establishes that the resulting value measures the intended construct.

# 4. Measurement Ontology

The minimum ontology contains the following entities and relations.

Construct: a theoretical property, relation, process, or outcome to be
investigated.\
Measurand: the specific quantity or attribute intended to be measured in
a declared case.\
Unit of analysis: the entity or aggregate to which the measurement is
attributed, such as event, action, episode, participant, dyad, system,
task, session, or population.\
Level of analysis: the temporal, organizational, representational, or
social level at which the claim is made.\
Observation: a recorded state, event, signal, report, or trace element
obtained through a declared observation process.\
Instrument: the mechanism that produces or records observations,
including logger, sensor, questionnaire, protocol, annotator, or system
model.\
Operationalization: the rule connecting a construct to observable
indicators and transformations.\
Indicator: an observable or derived variable used as evidence about a
construct.\
Score: a numerical or categorical representation produced by the
measurement procedure.\
Scale: the mathematical structure and permissible transformations
governing the score.\
Estimator: a procedure that infers an unknown quantity from
observations.\
Uncertainty: quantified incompleteness of knowledge about the measurand
or score interpretation.\
Validity argument: the evidence and reasoning supporting an intended
interpretation and use.\
Reliability: consistency of scores under declared replications, not
truth or validity.\
Comparison scope: the population, task, context, projection, and
tolerance under which scores may be compared.\
Decision rule: a threshold or mapping from measurements to
classifications or actions.\
Evidence record: a traceable package containing observations,
transformations, assumptions, and uncertainty.

The core relation is not construct -\> metric. It is:

Construct -\> operationalization -\> observation process -\>
observations -\> transformation or estimator -\> score -\>
interpretation.

Validity and uncertainty apply across this chain, not only to the final
score.

# 5. Observable, Derived, and Latent Variables

Interaction measurements should be classified by epistemic status.

Directly recorded variables are produced by a declared instrument with
minimal semantic transformation: timestamps, event identifiers, system
states, command invocations, pointer coordinates, sensor values, text
responses, and explicit ratings. They remain instrument- and
boundary-dependent.

Coded observations apply a rule to raw records: error type, action
category, recovery event, strategy segment, or successful transition.
Coding introduces a model and may require inter-rater or algorithmic
reliability.

Derived variables are deterministic or explicitly statistical
transformations of observations: duration, path length, transition
count, error rate, entropy, precision, recall, edit distance, or
proportion successful. Derivation does not by itself validate the
construct interpretation.

Model-based estimates are quantities inferred under a probabilistic or
computational model: latent state, posterior belief, workload estimate,
policy parameter, hazard, random effect, or predicted success
probability. Their meaning depends on model assumptions,
identifiability, calibration, and fit.

Latent constructs are theoretical variables not directly observed:
confidence, understanding, intention, trust, discoverability, cognitive
workload, strategy, perceived opportunity, or expertise. They require
multiple indicators, experimental interventions, convergent and
discriminant evidence, or a validated measurement model. A single
behavioral event cannot ordinarily identify a latent construct.

Interpretive conclusions are claims about mechanisms or causes. They are
not measurements, even when based on measured variables.

# 6. Construct Validity

Construct validity is the central problem for interaction measurement
because many target constructs are indirect. Cronbach and Meehl require
a network of theoretical relations connecting the construct to
observations and other constructs. Messick further treats validity as an
integrated argument about score meaning and use, rather than a property
possessed by an instrument in isolation.

A defensible interaction measurement should address:

Content relevance: indicators sample the intended construct rather than
a convenient proxy.\
Structural validity: the scoring or latent-variable structure matches
the proposed construct structure.\
Convergent evidence: different methods intended to measure the same
construct show the expected relationship.\
Discriminant evidence: the measure is separable from adjacent
constructs.\
Criterion relations: scores relate to external outcomes as theory
predicts.\
Known-groups or intervention evidence: manipulations expected to change
the construct change the score, while controls do not.\
Process evidence: the observation-generating process matches the
proposed interpretation.\
Generalization: score meaning remains stable across relevant
populations, tasks, contexts, and projections.\
Consequential validity: intended uses and foreseeable misuses are
evaluated where scores guide decisions.

No single correlation establishes validity. Validation is cumulative and
claim-specific. A measure may be valid for comparing discovery time
within one task yet invalid for ranking general interface quality.

# 7. Reliability, Reproducibility, and Generalizability

Reliability concerns consistency under repeated measurement conditions.
It may include temporal stability, internal consistency, inter-rater
agreement, inter-instrument agreement, or repeated-trial consistency.
High reliability is necessary for many comparisons but is not sufficient
for validity; a logger can record the wrong event with perfect
consistency.

Reproducibility requires sufficient specification for independent
researchers to implement the measurement process and obtain results
consistent within declared uncertainty. Computational interaction
studies should preserve event schemas, clocks, task definitions,
exclusions, preprocessing, coding manuals, estimator specifications,
software versions, and analysis decisions.

Generalizability concerns variation across persons, tasks, items,
systems, contexts, and occasions. A score is not automatically an
attribute of a person or interface. Many HCI measures are relational
properties of users, goals, systems, and contexts. Generalizability
theory and multilevel models are therefore more appropriate than
treating all variance outside the focal factor as undifferentiated
error.

A measurement report should state the intended universe of
generalization and identify which facets were sampled, fixed,
randomized, or omitted.

# 8. Uncertainty

Uncertainty in interaction research has several sources.

Instrument uncertainty includes clock resolution, event loss, sensor
error, sampling jitter, synchronization drift, and annotation interface
constraints.

Operational uncertainty arises from ambiguous event boundaries, task
completion rules, segmentation, and competing operational definitions.

Sampling uncertainty concerns persons, tasks, items, sessions, and
contexts.

Model uncertainty concerns functional form, priors, unobserved
confounding, missing data, identifiability, and estimator choice.

Construct uncertainty concerns whether the indicators support the
intended latent interpretation.

Context uncertainty concerns whether measurements transfer across
projections, devices, languages, cultures, expertise levels, and
environments.

Decision uncertainty concerns thresholds and the consequences of false
classifications.

An uncertainty budget should list each source, its treatment, and
whether it is quantified, bounded, sensitivity-tested, or unresolved.
Confidence intervals alone do not cover model, construct, or scope
uncertainty.

# 9. Canonical Metric Families

No universal scalar interaction metric is supported. The literature
instead supports typed metric families.

Temporal metrics: latency, duration, inter-event interval, dwell,
recovery time, learning rate, and time-to-discovery.

Outcome metrics: task success, transition success, goal attainment,
partial completion, quality, safety, and persistence of effects.

Error metrics: error count, error probability, severity, detectability,
correction rate, escalation, and residual harm.

Path and sequence metrics: action count, path length, edit distance,
state coverage, branching, backtracking, sequence entropy, and
conformance to a declared model.

Opportunity metrics: precision and recall of believed actions against
executable actions, discovery probability, exposure coverage, signaling
calibration, reachable-outcome coverage, and recovery visibility.

Information metrics: entropy, mutual information, uncertainty reduction,
channel capacity, and coding cost, only when the random variables and
probabilistic assumptions are defined. Shannon information does not
measure meaning, understanding, or usefulness by itself.

Resource metrics: physical effort, attentional demand, memory demand,
computational cost, energy, bandwidth, and coordination load.

Subjective measures: perceived workload, confidence, trust,
satisfaction, risk, usability, and perceived reversibility. These are
reports under a measurement model, not transparent readings of internal
state.

Comparative metrics: effect size, equivalence bounds, calibration
difference, distributional distance, and invariance tests.

Each metric must be tied to a construct card. Metrics should not be
combined into an index unless the aggregation rule and trade-offs are
theoretically justified.

# 10. Measurement Contracts

Every reported interaction measure should be accompanied by a
measurement contract containing:

1\. Construct and intended interpretation.\
2. Measurand and unit of analysis.\
3. Scope conditions: population, task, system, projection, context, and
time.\
4. Observation model and instrument.\
5. Event, state, and boundary definitions.\
6. Operationalization and indicators.\
7. Transformation, coding, or estimator.\
8. Scale type and permissible operations.\
9. Missingness, exclusions, and preprocessing.\
10. Reliability evidence.\
11. Validity evidence.\
12. Uncertainty budget.\
13. Comparison and invariance assumptions.\
14. Failure conditions and prohibited interpretations.\
15. Reproducibility artifacts.

This contract is the minimum reusable unit of measurement specification.
It makes the evidential chain inspectable and supports later
interaction-similarity and comparative-interaction research.

# 11. Comparability and Measurement Invariance

Two scores are comparable only when they preserve an intended
interpretation across the cases being compared. Numerical equality is
insufficient. The same completion time can arise from different task
boundaries, clocks, path constraints, or strategies. The same
questionnaire total can have different factor structures or response
meanings across populations.

Comparability requires at least:

Construct identity: the same construct interpretation is intended.\
Operational correspondence: indicators and coding rules have equivalent
roles.\
Scale compatibility: permissible transformations and units are aligned.\
Measurement invariance: item or indicator relations remain stable where
latent scores are compared.\
Context declaration: task, goals, authority, projection, and environment
are controlled or modeled.\
Sampling alignment: populations and units are comparable or adjusted.\
Uncertainty compatibility: uncertainty is reported on commensurate
terms.\
Tolerance: equivalence is defined by a prespecified practically
meaningful bound.

When these conditions fail, the correct result is typed
non-comparability, not forced normalization.

# 12. Experimental Framework

The recommended experimental framework separates construct,
intervention, measurement, and inference.

Phase 1 - Theory and construct specification. Define the construct,
competing explanations, unit and level of analysis, and causal role.

Phase 2 - Measurement design. Create construct cards, select indicators,
define events and boundaries, specify instruments, and preregister
uncertainty and exclusion rules.

Phase 3 - Manipulation and comparison design. Specify treatment,
control, manipulation checks, nuisance variables, and minimum meaningful
effects or equivalence bounds.

Phase 4 - Data generation. Record raw observations with provenance,
synchronized clocks, immutable event identifiers, and declared
missingness.

Phase 5 - Transformation and coding. Apply versioned rules; preserve
raw-to-derived traceability; assess rater or algorithmic agreement.

Phase 6 - Estimation. Fit models appropriate to nesting, repeated
measures, censoring, measurement error, and uncertainty. Avoid treating
participant or task variance as independent observations.

Phase 7 - Validation. Test convergent, discriminant, structural,
intervention, criterion, and generalization evidence.

Phase 8 - Sensitivity and falsification. Test alternative
operationalizations, priors, exclusions, model forms, and rival
mechanisms.

Phase 9 - Reporting. Publish the measurement contract, uncertainty
budget, analysis specification, and prohibited interpretations.

# 13. Evidence Taxonomy

Evidence should be reported by level.

Level 0 - Raw record: minimally processed event, signal, state, or
report.\
Level 1 - Verified observation: record checked for provenance,
integrity, timing, and instrument behavior.\
Level 2 - Coded observation: category assigned under a documented rule.\
Level 3 - Derived measure: deterministic or statistical summary of
observations.\
Level 4 - Model estimate: parameter, posterior, or latent score inferred
under a declared model.\
Level 5 - Construct evidence: multiple measures support an
interpretation of a theoretical construct.\
Level 6 - Mechanism evidence: interventions, temporal ordering, and
rival tests support a generating process.\
Level 7 - Generalized claim: evidence supports transfer across declared
populations, tasks, systems, or projections.

Higher levels depend on lower levels but do not become direct
observations. A mechanism claim should remain labeled as inference even
when strongly supported.

# 14. Falsification Tests

The framework should be narrowed or rejected if the following occur.

Measurement redundancy: established measurement theory can already
express every requirement without any interaction-specific coordination
artifact. In that case only a domain checklist, not a new framework, is
warranted.

Non-operational constructs: central interaction constructs cannot be
connected to observable indicators with discriminant validity.

No incremental validity: specialized opportunity, projection, or
interaction metrics fail to explain or predict outcomes beyond ordinary
task, system, and participant variables.

Invariance failure: measures change interpretation across projections,
populations, or tasks despite apparent numerical comparability.

Observer dependence without calibration: event boundaries and coding
cannot achieve reproducible agreement.

Uncertainty dominance: measurement and model uncertainty exceed the
effects under investigation.

Causal ambiguity: proposed mechanisms remain indistinguishable from
simpler rival explanations under intervention.

Metric instability: conclusions reverse under equally defensible
operationalizations or preprocessing choices.

The framework survives only if it improves traceability, construct
validity, and comparative inference relative to untyped metric
reporting.

# 15. Threats to Validity

The synthesis risks over-formalizing phenomena that are situated,
socially negotiated, or emergent. Not every meaningful interaction
property is naturally scalar. Qualitative observations may provide
stronger construct evidence than forced quantification.

Measurement contracts can create procedural compliance without genuine
validity. Explicit fields do not substitute for theory or empirical
validation.

The framework inherits disputes within measurement theory, including
whether all measurement requires numerical structural representation and
how causal accounts of measurement relate to representational accounts.

HCI constructs often depend on context of use. Generalization across
tasks, cultures, languages, accessibility conditions, and expertise may
be limited. Measurement invariance may fail for theoretically meaningful
reasons rather than instrument defects.

Instrumentation can change the phenomenon being measured through
reactivity, latency, logging overhead, surveillance effects, or task
restructuring.

Finally, evidence quality is not reducible to a linear hierarchy.
Different questions require different forms of evidence; the taxonomy
records dependency and inferential distance, not universal superiority.

# 16. Implications for Interaction Research

The measurement framework completes the transition from conceptual
ontology to empirical research. Prior work distinguishes ontology,
semantics, representation, interpretation, opportunity, interaction, and
behavior. Measurement adds the rules by which claims about these
constructs can be connected to evidence without collapsing them.

For representation research, it requires typed equivalence tests and
invariance conditions. For opportunity research, it separates
executable, exposed, signaled, believed, selected, and successful
actions into different measurands. For behavior research, it converts
traces into evidence through declared segmentation and coding. For
interaction comparison, it supplies equivalence bounds and comparability
tests. For prediction, it separates measurement quality from model
performance.

The central implication is that computational interaction research
should stop treating metric labels as self-interpreting. Time, error,
success, workload, trust, discoverability, and usability are valid only
through explicit measurement contracts.

# 17. Conclusion

Existing measurement theory, psychometrics, metrology, statistics,
experimental psychology, HCI evaluation, and systems engineering are
sufficient to explain how interaction phenomena can be measured. No new
foundational theory of measurement is required.

A domain-specific synthesis is nevertheless necessary because
interaction research combines system events, behavioral traces,
subjective reports, relational constructs, and latent interpretations in
ways that invite category errors. The warranted contribution is a shared
measurement architecture, not a new measurement primitive.

The primary conclusion is:

Interaction phenomena should be measured through explicit contracts
linking constructs to observation processes, transformations,
uncertainty, validity evidence, and comparison scope. Observations,
derived metrics, latent estimates, and explanatory conclusions must
remain typed and traceable throughout the evidential chain.

1\. Define construct, rival explanations, unit, and level.

2\. Create construct card and measurement contract.

3\. Specify treatment, control, manipulation check, nuisance variables,

5\. Apply versioned coding and transformation rules.

6\. Estimate with models appropriate to nesting, censoring, and
