**Formal Models of Computational Interaction**

*Toward a Mathematical Foundation*

Cross-disciplinary foundational research paper

# Abstract

This paper evaluates whether one established formalism can represent the
interaction theory developed across prior work on ontology, semantics,
representation, projection, opportunity, behavior, measurement,
similarity, transfer, and strategy. Labeled transition systems, Petri
nets, process algebras, statecharts, event structures, workflow nets,
Markov decision processes, partially observable Markov decision
processes, category-theoretic process models, and multi-agent formalisms
are compared by a common set of obligations: bounded interaction
episodes, reciprocal coupling, partial-order behavior, typed
opportunity, projection and observation, latent strategy, uncertainty,
empirical traces, composition, and typed equivalence.

No candidate satisfies every obligation without extension. Labeled
transition systems provide the smallest operational core and the
broadest verification ecosystem, but interleaving semantics obscures
true concurrency and standard forms omit observation, policy,
measurement, and empirical uncertainty. Event structures preserve
causality, conflict, and concurrency but are less convenient for
state-rich, stochastic, and instrumented systems. Petri nets and
workflow nets excel at concurrency, resources, and completion. Process
algebras provide the strongest native composition and behavioral
equivalence theory. MDPs and POMDPs provide decision, uncertainty,
belief, and strategy semantics but ordinarily presuppose a fixed
action/state model and weakly represent organizational and
representational structure. Statecharts provide hierarchy and practical
specification but lack one universally accepted mathematical semantics.
Category theory supplies a principled language of composition and
translation rather than a sufficient empirical model by itself.

The evidence therefore supports a conservative hybrid foundation rather
than a new calculus: an observation-enriched probabilistic labeled
transition system as the canonical semantic kernel; event-structure or
Petri-net views for concurrent causality and resource flow;
process-algebraic operators for composition and equivalence; and
POMDP-style belief and policy layers where agency under uncertainty is
part of the explanandum. A trace-and-measurement morphism connects
formal executions to empirical records. The paper supplies a formal
ontology mapping, core semantics, model comparison matrix,
expressiveness analysis, and recommended foundation.

# 1. Problem Statement

The established interaction theory imposes obligations that exceed
ordinary interface-state modeling. An interaction episode has declared
participants, boundary, timescale, coupling, preconditions, transitions,
invariants, evidence, failure, recovery, and completion. Behavior is a
bounded attributed trajectory under an observation model rather than raw
telemetry. Opportunity distinguishes domain-valid, capable, permitted,
enabled, reachable, exposed, signaled, believed, executable, successful,
and reversible action. Strategy is a latent, temporally extended
organization of conditional action selection. Measurement connects
records to variables and claims through explicit operationalization and
uncertainty. Similarity is typed rather than universal.

A formal foundation must preserve these distinctions while remaining
analyzable and compositional. The central problem is not which formalism
is most expressive in the abstract. It is which minimal combination
represents the established ontology without encoding every distinction
as an informal annotation or inventing a new mathematical language.

# 2. Evaluation Method

Each candidate formalism was evaluated against the same representation
obligations. The assessment distinguishes native expressiveness from
expressibility by arbitrary encoding. A universal programming language
can encode nearly any finite model, but such encodability does not make
its semantics transparent or its analyses appropriate.

The criteria were: (1) episode boundaries and identity; (2) state and
transition semantics; (3) reciprocity and coupling; (4) concurrency and
causal independence; (5) nondeterminism; (6) probability and
uncertainty; (7) partial observability and projection; (8) opportunity
and authorization; (9) policy and strategy; (10) empirical trace
alignment; (11) composition and decomposition; (12) equivalence and
refinement; (13) verification and quantitative analysis; and (14)
suitability for estimation from observed interaction data.

The review prioritized foundational sources: labeled transition systems
and model checking; Murata on Petri nets; Milner on process algebra;
Harel on statecharts; Winskel on event structures; workflow-net
soundness; Sutton and Barto on MDPs; Kaelbling, Littman, and Cassandra
on POMDPs; and categorical process semantics. The conclusion is
comparative and architectural, not a claim that all systems should be
implemented using one notation.

# 3. Formal Obligations Derived from the Theory

The formal object must distinguish six kinds of state: domain state,
participant state, authority state, projection state, observer or belief
state, and measurement state. Combining them into one Cartesian state is
mathematically possible but destroys explanatory modularity and causes
state-space explosion. The foundation should therefore permit factored
state and typed transition labels.

An interaction episode requires more than a transition path. It requires
a boundary predicate, participant assignment, coupling relation,
initiating and completion conditions, and evidence linking the modeled
episode to observations. Reciprocal constraint need not mean
simultaneous bidirectional transition. It can be represented by causal
dependence across a bounded execution: an event of one participant
changes the enabled, probable, observable, or valued future of another,
whose subsequent event recurrently constrains the first or the shared
system.

Opportunity requires multiple predicates over actions and states rather
than one action set. Projection and observation require mappings from
domain states and transitions to exposed operations and observable
symbols. Belief requires probability or possibility over hidden states.
Strategy requires a policy-like object over histories, observations, or
beliefs, plus temporally extended organization where needed. Empirical
use requires a stochastic or uncertain observation channel from
executions to records.

# 4. Labeled Transition Systems

A labeled transition system (LTS) consists minimally of states, action
labels, and a transition relation. It provides the clearest common
denominator for enabled actions, executions, traces, reachability,
safety, liveness, refinement, simulation, and bisimulation. Interaction
episodes can be represented as bounded executions satisfying initiation
and completion predicates. Typed labels can identify actor, channel,
operation, authorization result, and outcome.

The principal strength of LTS semantics is analyzability. Model
checking, equivalence checking, reachability, temporal logic, and
compositional reductions are mature. LTSs also serve as semantic targets
for statecharts, process algebras, workflow systems, and many
programming languages.

The limitations are equally important. Standard interleaving semantics
represents concurrent events as alternative sequences and therefore
loses causal independence unless enriched. Ordinary LTSs do not natively
distinguish projection from domain state, observation from execution,
permission from enablement, policy from transition availability, or
empirical records from formal traces. Probability, time, cost, and
partial observability require extensions. The LTS is therefore the best
semantic kernel, not a complete interaction model.

# 5. Petri Nets and Workflow Nets

Petri nets represent distributed state through places and tokens and
behavior through transition firing. They are particularly strong for
concurrency, synchronization, resource consumption, conflict,
invariants, boundedness, liveness, and reachability. Their graphical and
algebraic structure makes them well suited to workflows, multi-party
protocols, and interactions in which independent activities and shared
resources matter.

Workflow nets add distinguished source and sink conditions and support
soundness questions concerning completion, residual tokens, and dead
transitions. These concepts correspond naturally to interaction
initiation, completion, deadlock, and cleanup.

Standard place-transition nets remain weak for rich data, hierarchical
projection, belief, policy, and measurement. Colored, timed, stochastic,
and inhibitor-arc variants increase expressiveness but fragment analysis
and can approach general programming-language complexity. Petri nets
should therefore be treated as a concurrent-resource view of the
canonical model, especially where partial-order structure and completion
are central.

# 6. Process Algebras

Process algebras such as CCS, CSP, and the pi-calculus represent systems
through processes and operators for action prefix, choice, parallel
composition, synchronization, hiding, relabeling, and recursion. Their
major contribution is not simply another transition notation; it is a
compositional theory in which the behavior of a whole can be derived
from interacting parts and compared through rigorously defined
observational relations.

This is highly aligned with the interaction theory. Participant
processes can be composed through channels, internal actions can be
hidden, projections can be modeled by abstraction or renaming, and typed
equivalences can express what an observer can distinguish. Process
algebra offers the strongest native account of compositional interaction
identity and substitutability.

Classic process algebras are less natural for quantitative human
behavior, empirical traces, continuous variables, resources, belief, and
learning. Probabilistic, timed, stochastic, and hybrid variants exist,
but no single process calculus has become the universal
cross-disciplinary foundation. Process algebra is best used to define
composition, interface contracts, and equivalence over the transition
kernel.

# 7. Statecharts

Statecharts extend state machines with hierarchy, orthogonality, and
broadcast communication. These features address practical complexity:
hierarchical states support abstraction; orthogonal regions represent
concurrency; history supports resumption; and event-triggered
transitions support reactive behavior. They are highly usable for
engineered interactive systems and can align naturally with interface
modes and lifecycle states.

Their weakness as a foundational theory is semantic plurality. Variants
differ in event queues, step semantics, priority, run-to-completion,
concurrency, and history. Statecharts can be translated into transition
systems, but the resulting semantics must be declared explicitly. They
are therefore an effective authoring and presentation notation rather
than the canonical mathematical substrate.

# 8. Event Structures

Event structures represent computations as event occurrences constrained
by causality, consistency, enabling, and conflict. They distinguish true
concurrency from mere nondeterministic interleaving and make
partial-order traces primary. This is valuable for interaction because
logs often impose a total order that is not causally justified, and
because distributed or collaborative episodes contain independent
events.

Event structures also support counterfactual questions about which
events depend on which prior events and which alternatives exclude one
another. These relations are closer to the interaction paper's
recurrent-constraint account than a flat sequence is.

However, event structures are less direct for mutable data-rich state,
continuous quantities, reward, partial observation, and online
estimation. Probabilistic and game extensions exist, but tool ecosystems
are narrower. Event structures should be available as a
causal-concurrency semantics derived from or linked to the transition
kernel.

# 9. MDPs and POMDPs

A Markov decision process represents states, actions, transition
probabilities, rewards, and policies. It directly supports stochastic
behavior, expected outcomes, controllability through action, and
strategy evaluation. A partially observable MDP adds observations and
belief states, making it especially relevant to the distinction between
actual state, projection, observation, believed actions, and expected
consequences.

These formalisms are the strongest candidates for opportunity, strategy,
adaptation, and prediction. A projection can be represented partly
through the observation kernel and available action function; belief
mediates action selection; options can represent temporally extended
policies.

Their standard assumptions create limits. The Markov property may
require state augmentation. A single optimizing agent and scalar reward
may misrepresent collaborative, institutional, or interpretive
interaction. Authorization, signaling, semantics, and measurement
validity are not intrinsic. POMDP observations are probabilistic
signals, not the complete concept of representation or projection.
MDP/POMDP semantics should therefore be an optional decision layer over
the interaction kernel, not the universal ontology.

# 10. Category-Theoretic Process Models

Category theory provides objects, morphisms, composition, identity,
products, monoidal structure, functors, and natural transformations. In
process-oriented applications, objects can represent interfaces or
systems and morphisms can represent processes. Symmetric monoidal
categories support parallel composition and diagrammatic reasoning.
Functors can relate different semantic models while preserving
composition.

This makes category theory valuable for expressing the architecture of
the research program: multiple views of one interaction model,
compositional contracts, translations between Petri nets and execution
categories, and preservation claims across projections. It is
particularly suited to stating when a translation is structure
preserving.

Category theory does not by itself choose the empirical entities,
transition probabilities, observation model, or measurement semantics.
Treating it as the primary model would move essential commitments into
the choice of category. It should therefore serve as a meta-level
compositional and translation framework, not the sole executable
semantics.

# 11. Multi-Agent and Game-Based Models

Multi-agent systems represent multiple agents with local states,
actions, observations, protocols, knowledge, goals, and sometimes
utilities. Concurrent game structures add strategic choice and
adversarial or cooperative outcomes. Epistemic and temporal logics can
express what agents know and what coalitions can enforce.

These models directly address distributed agency and asymmetric
opportunity. They can represent authorization, imperfect information,
joint action, coordination, negotiation, and strategic interaction
better than single-agent MDPs.

Their limitation is heterogeneity: multi-agent modeling is a family of
frameworks rather than one semantics. Agent identity, rationality,
knowledge, communication, and utility assumptions vary widely. The
recommended foundation should permit multiple participant policies and
local observation models without presupposing ideal rational agents or
equilibrium behavior.

# 12. Comparative Result

No single candidate dominates across all obligations. LTSs lead on
minimality, operational clarity, verification, and equivalence. Process
algebras lead on native composition and observational substitutability.
Event structures and Petri nets lead on true concurrency, causality, and
resource flow. Statecharts lead on practical hierarchical specification.
POMDPs lead on partial observability, belief, policy, and stochastic
decision. Category theory leads on compositional translation across
models.

The comparison rejects two alternatives. A monolithic Cartesian-state
POMDP can encode nearly every distinction but makes ontology, authority,
representation, measurement, and composition opaque. A purely
process-algebraic foundation captures interaction structure but leaves
empirical uncertainty, belief, and data-model alignment as external
additions. The minimal defensible solution is therefore a layered
semantic profile with one canonical kernel and formally related views.

# 13. Recommended Formal Foundation

The recommended kernel is an observation-enriched probabilistic labeled
transition system (OEPLTS):

M = \<N, S, A, T, I, F, C, P, X, O, Y, R\>.

N is the set of participants and system components. S is a factored
state space. A is a typed action/event vocabulary. T(s,a,s\') is a
nondeterministic or probabilistic transition relation. I and F define
episode initiation and completion. C defines effective capability. P
defines authorization. X defines exposure through a projection. O maps
hidden state and events to observer-accessible observations. Y maps
executions to instrument records. R defines recovery or reversibility
relations.

A participant-relative strategy is a history-, observation-, or
belief-dependent policy pi_i. Belief update is added when O is
non-injective or stochastic. Rewards or criteria are optional and typed
rather than mandatory. A coupling relation K identifies cross-component
dependencies by which an event or state change of one component alters
another component\'s enabled transitions, transition probabilities,
observations, or value-relevant futures.

The kernel has three associated semantics. Its unfolding into an event
structure provides causal and concurrent semantics. Its composition
through process-algebraic operators provides modular semantics and
behavioral equivalences. Its decision enrichment into an MDP, POMDP,
stochastic game, or decentralized POMDP provides policy and uncertainty
semantics. Petri-net or workflow projections represent resource and
completion structure. Category-theoretic functors can state preservation
across these views.

Empirical linkage is explicit: an execution omega generates an
observation trace through O and an instrument record through Y.
Segmentation and attribution functions turn records into behavioral
events under a measurement contract. This prevents formal traces from
being equated automatically with observed behavior.

# 14. Formal Semantics

An execution is a finite or infinite alternating sequence s0, a0, s1,
a1, \... satisfying T. An interaction episode is an execution segment
bounded by I and F in which the declared coupling criterion K is
satisfied. Reciprocity is tested over the causal dependency graph, not
merely by the presence of actions from multiple actors.

The executable set for participant i at state s is the intersection of
domain-valid, capable, permitted, and enabled actions. Exposure and
signaling are additional projection-relative predicates and need not
coincide with executability. Believed availability is defined over the
participant\'s belief state and may include false positives or omit
executable actions.

Composition is defined by synchronized product over shared labels or
explicit channels, with hiding and relabeling. Independent transitions
may interleave operationally but are retained as concurrent in the
event-structure unfolding. Refinement is typed: trace inclusion,
simulation, bisimulation, probabilistic bisimulation, testing
equivalence, opportunity preservation, or measurement-relative
equivalence must be selected explicitly.

The model is implementation independent. A GUI, CLI, API, conversational
agent, robot, or collaborative workflow is represented through different
projection, observation, and action mappings over a declared domain and
transition semantics.

# 15. Analyzability and Empirical Suitability

The recommended kernel preserves access to mature algorithms:
reachability, invariant checking, temporal-logic model checking,
simulation and bisimulation checking, probabilistic model checking,
controller synthesis, policy evaluation, and partial-order reduction.
Factored state and modular composition are necessary to reduce state
explosion.

Empirical suitability requires a different set of checks. Model states
and labels must be operationally linked to records; hidden variables
must not be treated as observed; timing and missingness must be
represented; and parameter estimates must carry uncertainty. Conformance
between traces and models should distinguish deviation, observation
error, abstraction error, and model misspecification.

The formal model is therefore not itself a measurement instrument. It is
a theory-constrained representation whose empirical use depends on a
measurement contract, estimation procedure, and validation evidence.

# 16. Falsification and Threats to Validity

The recommendation should be rejected or narrowed if a single
established formalism can represent all required distinctions natively,
preserve modularity, support the necessary analyses, and connect to
empirical records without ad hoc layers. It should also be rejected if
the proposed mappings cannot be made semantics-preserving or if
independent analysts cannot reproduce the ontology-to-model mapping.

A second threat is over-formalization. Human interaction boundaries,
intentions, semantics, and social rules may be contested or emergent.
Formal precision does not eliminate uncertainty about what should be
modeled. A third threat is state explosion and undecidability: increased
expressiveness can destroy analyzability. A fourth is false realism: a
model can be internally coherent while omitting institutional,
environmental, or representational variables that generated observed
behavior.

The foundation therefore makes scope conditions explicit. It is
strongest for computationally mediated episodes with declared
operations, participants, records, and boundaries. Open-ended cultural
activity may require qualitative and historical explanation alongside
formal modeling.

# 17. Conclusion

The minimum adequate foundation is not a new universal calculus. It is a
conservative layered architecture centered on an observation-enriched
probabilistic labeled transition system. The LTS kernel supplies state,
transition, execution, reachability, and verification. Process algebra
supplies composition and typed behavioral equivalence. Event structures
or Petri nets supply concurrency, causality, and resource flow. POMDP or
game enrichments supply partial observation, belief, policy, and
stochastic strategy. Measurement mappings connect executions to records
and claims. Category theory can organize translations and preservation
across these views.

This recommendation preserves the strongest existing mathematics while
matching the conceptual distinctions already established. It also leaves
open an empirical test: if the layered model does not improve
specification, comparison, explanation, verification, or prediction
relative to simpler baselines, the additional structure should be
removed.

# 18. Reusable Artifacts

## C. Expressiveness Mapping

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  Required construct                  Recommended representation
  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Episode boundaries                  Predicates I and F over execution
                                      states/events

  Reciprocal coupling                 Dependency relation K over
                                      components, transitions,
                                      observations, or enabled sets

  Concurrency                         Event-structure unfolding or
                                      Petri-net projection; partial-order
                                      reduction

  Opportunity                         Typed state/action predicates C, P,
                                      E, X plus reachability and recovery

  Projection                          State-dependent mapping from domain
                                      model to exposed actions and
                                      observations

  Measurement                         Channel Y from execution to records
                                      plus segmentation/attribution
                                      functions

  Uncertainty                         Probabilistic transition and
                                      observation kernels; interval or
                                      imprecise variants where needed

  Strategy                            Policies over histories,
                                      observations, or beliefs; options
                                      for temporal extension

  Composition                         Synchronized product, parallel
                                      operator, hiding, relabeling,
                                      interface contracts

  Similarity/equivalence              Trace, simulation, bisimulation,
                                      testing, probabilistic,
                                      opportunity, and
                                      measurement-relative relations
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

## D. Recommended Formal Profile

Canonical kernel: observation-enriched probabilistic labeled transition
system.

Composition semantics: process-algebraic synchronized product, hiding,
relabeling, recursion, and typed equivalence.

Concurrency semantics: event-structure unfolding or Petri-net projection
when causal independence and resources matter.

Decision semantics: MDP, POMDP, stochastic-game, or decentralized
enrichment only when uncertainty, policy, or strategic choice is part of
the explanatory target.

Empirical semantics: observation channel and instrument-record channel
governed by the Measurement Contract and Behavioral Evidence Contract.

Translation semantics: explicit structure-preserving mappings between
views, optionally formalized as functors.

# The Limits of Computational Interaction Models

**Version:** Draft 0.2  
**Project:** Foundations of Computational Interaction  
**Status:** Foundational Position Paper

---

# Abstract

Every scientific framework is defined not only by what it explains, but by what it refuses to claim.

This document establishes the epistemic boundaries for Foundations of Computational Interaction. It argues that interaction models should seek structure without determinism, formalization without false certainty, generality without reductionism, and integration without replacing adjacent disciplines.

The purpose of these limits is not to weaken the discipline. It is to make its claims scientifically defensible.

---

# 1. Why Boundaries Matter

New disciplines often fail by overextending their explanatory authority.

If Foundations of Computational Interaction attempts to explain culture, cognition, personality, intelligence, organizations, and society through interaction alone, it will become another grand unified theory with little empirical value.

Instead, the discipline should explicitly define where its authority begins and ends.

Interaction models explain interaction.

They do not explain people in their entirety.

---

# 2. Culture Does Not Determine Behavior

Culture shapes exposure, meaning, expectations, conventions, symbolism, and interaction practices.

It does not determine behavior.

The preferred model is:

```text
Cultural and community context
        ↓
changes probabilities of exposure,
meaning, expectation, and practice
        ↓
interacts with individual history,
task, representation, and situation
        ↓
contributes to behavior
```

Research should therefore investigate mechanisms rather than treating demographic identity as causal.

---

# 3. Interaction History Does Not Fully Explain Individuals

Accumulated interaction experience may improve explanation beyond demographic categories, but it is only one explanatory layer.

Behavior also depends upon:

- current objectives;
- domain knowledge;
- accessibility;
- fatigue;
- immediate context;
- consequences;
- uncertainty;
- individual variation.

Interaction Ecology should therefore remain probabilistic rather than deterministic.

```text
Behavior =
interaction history
× task
× representation
× opportunity
× immediate state
× individual variation
```

---

# 4. Interaction May Not Reduce to a Fixed Grammar

A canonical interaction grammar is valuable only if it preserves explanatory power.

Interaction may instead require a layered grammar.

```text
Input Form
↓

Semantic Action
↓

Situated Action
↓

Activity
```

The discipline should determine whether interaction possesses a finite primitive grammar, an extensible grammar, or no stable grammar at all.

---

# 5. Internal Cognition Cannot Be Directly Observed

Interaction systems observe behavior.

They do not observe beliefs, confidence, curiosity, understanding, trust, or intention directly.

Those remain latent constructs.

Every inference should preserve the distinction:

```text
Observed Behavior
        ↓
Behavioral Feature
        ↓
Candidate Interpretation
        ↓
Uncertainty
```

Behavior must never be silently promoted into psychology.

---

# 6. Representation Is Not the Only Cause of Behavior

Representation influences interaction.

It does not fully explain it.

Behavior emerges through multiple interacting factors.

```text
Behavior =
semantic state
× representation
× morphology
× interaction grammar
× opportunity structure
× agent state
× task
```

Representation should therefore be studied as one manipulated variable rather than the sole explanatory mechanism.

---

# 7. Formalization Does Not Eliminate Ambiguity

Ontologies, formal models, and computational systems improve reproducibility.

They do not eliminate ambiguity.

Formalization moves ambiguity into:

- construct definitions;
- event classification;
- opportunity boundaries;
- model assumptions;
- interpretation rules.

The contribution of formalization is not certainty.

Its contribution is inspectable uncertainty.

---

# 8. One Ontology Should Not Replace Existing Disciplines

Foundations of Computational Interaction should integrate findings across:

- Human–Computer Interaction;
- Psychology;
- Anthropology;
- Human Factors;
- Design;
- Information Science.

It should not replace them.

The ontology provides a shared relational structure through which findings become comparable.

---


# 9. Similarity Is Not a Universal Score

Interaction comparison is always relative to a target, frame, correspondence mapping, observables, admissible transformations, metrics, tolerances, uncertainty, and validity domain.

Semantic similarity does not establish opportunity, behavioral, strategy, causal, or measurement similarity. When a defensible common comparison space cannot be established, the result is incomparability rather than a forced ranking.

# 10. A Trace Does Not Reveal a Strategy

Strategies are latent explanatory constructs. A repeated sequence supports a descriptive regularity, not by itself a plan, policy, intention, habit, or strategy.

Scientific strategy attribution requires rival models, diagnostic contingencies, uncertainty, repeated evidence, and preferably intervention or out-of-sample discrimination.

# 11. A Metric Is Not a Construct

A numerical measure does not become comprehension, confidence, expertise, trust, quality, or accessibility merely by being renamed. Every measurement claim must declare its measurand, observation process, operationalization, scale, uncertainty, validity evidence, population, task, projection, and permitted interpretation.

# 12. Contracts Do Not Eliminate Judgment

Projection, Opportunity, Interaction, Behavioral Evidence, Measurement, Similarity, and Strategy Contracts make assumptions inspectable. They do not eliminate boundary choices, coding judgment, model selection, interpretation, or uncertainty.

# 13. A Doctrine of Bounded Explanation

Foundations of Computational Interaction should adopt the following doctrine:

- Seek structure without determinism.
- Seek formalization without false certainty.
- Seek generality without reductionism.
- Seek integration without disciplinary replacement.
- Preserve uncertainty rather than concealing it.
- Distinguish observation from interpretation.
- Prefer mechanisms over categories.

These principles define the epistemic limits of the discipline.

---

# 14. Conclusion

The long-term credibility of Foundations of Computational Interaction will depend as much on the claims it refuses to make as the claims it advances.

A disciplined ontology should clarify what interaction models can explain, what they may only suggest, and what remains outside their authority.

Those boundaries are not weaknesses.

They are prerequisites for scientific rigor.

==============================================================================

**Predicting Interaction**

*Toward a Predictive Theory of Computational Interaction*

Formal research paper

# Abstract

Computational interaction is predictively tractable only under declared
targets, horizons, observation models, populations, interventions, and
loss functions. Existing research supplies successful local predictive
laws and models: Fitts\' law predicts constrained movement time;
Hick-Hyman relations predict choice latency under controlled
alternatives; GOMS and the Model Human Processor predict skilled task
time; cognitive architectures generate task-specific performance
trajectories; Bayesian, survival, sequential, and machine-learning
models forecast events under uncertainty. These successes do not
establish a universal predictive theory. Discovery, errors, recovery,
abandonment, adaptation, expertise, transfer, and strategy differ in
observability, temporal scale, causal dependence, and distributional
stability. Prediction must therefore be typed.

This paper distinguishes forecasting from explanation, retrodiction,
diagnosis, causal effect estimation, and intervention planning. It
proposes a prediction ontology and a layered framework in which
predictions are conditional distributions over declared interaction
targets generated from episode state, opportunity structure, projection,
behavioral history, agent experience, strategy hypotheses, and context.
Predictive claims must report calibration, discrimination, decision
utility, uncertainty, transport conditions, and failure criteria. The
central conclusion is that computational interaction supports predictive
science, but only as a family of scoped, probabilistic, and updateable
models. Low-level performance and near-term transitions are often
strongly predictable; higher-order constructs and long-horizon outcomes
are forecastable only as distributions and frequently remain
unidentified without intervention or richer observation.

# 1. Problem Statement

The preceding research program defines interaction episodes, behavioral
traces, opportunity profiles, strategies, transfer, similarity, and a
measurement architecture. Prediction is the next test of whether these
constructs support empirical science rather than only conceptual
organization. The relevant question is not whether some interaction
outcomes correlate with earlier variables. It is whether future or
unobserved interaction variables can be forecast with known uncertainty
under declared conditions and whether the resulting forecasts remain
valid across participants, tasks, projections, time, and interventions.

Interaction is an especially difficult predictive domain. The system and
agent mutually constrain later trajectories; observations are partial;
behavior changes beliefs and opportunity; participants learn; interfaces
and policies change; and the prediction itself may alter behavior.
Prediction targets also occupy different levels. A movement time is
directly measurable, while a strategy, expertise state, or believed
action set is latent. A model can predict a trace without explaining its
mechanism, explain a mechanism without predicting held-out traces, or
estimate an intervention effect without accurately predicting individual
outcomes.

The central research problem is therefore to define a disciplined
predictive architecture that separates target types, horizons,
information sets, causal questions, uncertainty, and validity domains.
The objective is not one universal model. It is the minimum framework
required to state, test, compare, update, and falsify predictive claims
about computational interaction.

# 2. Literature Review Method

The review was organized by predictive function rather than by
discipline. Primary and foundational sources were prioritized for:
statistical distinctions between explanation and prediction;
human-performance laws; engineering models of skilled interaction;
cognitive architectures; Bayesian and sequential models; machine
learning; survival and event-history analysis; causal inference;
transfer and transport; and predictive uncertainty. The earlier
Interaction, Behavior, Measurement, Opportunity, Similarity, Transfer,
Strategy, and Formal Models papers were treated as constraints on the
predictive target and evidence model, not as evidence that prediction
must succeed.

Each tradition was evaluated against five questions: What is predicted?
From what information? At what horizon and unit? Under what assumptions?
By what evidence is success or failure established? Claims were rejected
as predictive when they were evaluated only in-sample, used future
information, relied on post-outcome labels, lacked a baseline, or did
not report uncertainty and calibration.

# 3. Explanation, Prediction, and Intervention

Prediction and explanation are distinct scientific aims. Predictive
modeling minimizes expected loss for unobserved cases under a specified
data-generating regime. Explanatory modeling aims to identify or support
mechanisms, causes, or theoretical dependencies. A structurally faithful
explanatory model can predict poorly when unmodeled variability
dominates, while a flexible predictor can forecast accurately without
identifying the generating mechanism. This distinction is emphasized by
Shmueli and by Yarkoni and Westfall.

Four additional functions must remain separate:

-   Retrodiction estimates an unobserved or hidden past variable from
    later evidence.

-   Diagnosis classifies or explains a current condition from
    observations.

-   Causal effect estimation predicts the distribution that would follow
    an intervention rather than passive observation.

-   Decision or control selects an intervention using predicted
    consequences and utilities.

Observational prediction estimates P(Y_future \| H_observed).
Intervention prediction estimates P(Y_future \| do(A=a), H_observed).
The latter cannot generally be obtained from the former without causal
assumptions, identification conditions, or experimental variation. A
system that accurately predicts abandonment from frustration signals
does not thereby establish that reducing those signals will prevent
abandonment.

# 5. What Is Predictable?

Predictability is not a property of a phenomenon alone. It is a relation
among target, horizon, information set, population, observation process,
model class, and tolerance. The same outcome may be highly predictable
at the population level and weakly predictable for an individual.
Aggregate movement time may follow a stable law while a particular
person\'s next action remains uncertain.

# 6. Predictive Traditions

## 6.1 Human-performance laws

Fitts\' law and Hick-Hyman relations demonstrate that constrained
components of interaction can support compact, quantitative prediction.
Their scientific value comes from declared task structure, measurable
variables, reproducible relations, and explicit residual variation.
Their limitation is scope: they predict selected performance dimensions
under particular action and choice structures, not whole interactions.

## 6.2 Engineering models of interaction

GOMS, the Keystroke-Level Model, and the Model Human Processor predict
skilled, largely error-free task performance from decomposed operators
and processing assumptions. They are strongest when methods and
operators are known and weakest when discovery, learning,
interpretation, collaboration, interruption, or strategy change
dominates.

## 6.3 Cognitive architectures

ACT-R, EPIC, and related architectures generate predictions by
instantiating mechanistic assumptions about memory, perception,
cognition, and action. They can explain and predict within modeled
tasks, but performance depends on task encoding, model construction,
parameter selection, and whether the architecture captures the relevant
environmental coupling. Architecture-level commitments do not remove the
need for out-of-sample validation.

## 6.4 Bayesian and sequential models

Bayesian models express uncertainty over states, parameters, hypotheses,
and future observations. State-space models, hidden Markov models, MDPs,
and POMDPs are natural for interaction because they distinguish latent
state, observation, action, transition, and belief. They become
predictive only after the transition and observation models are
estimated or constrained, and their validity depends on stationarity and
state sufficiency.

## 6.5 Machine learning

Machine learning expands predictive capacity through flexible
representation and regularized out-of-sample optimization. It is
appropriate for heterogeneous traces, nonlinear interactions, and
high-dimensional histories. It does not automatically provide causal
interpretation, transportability, or calibrated uncertainty. Strong
performance within a random split may conceal failure across users,
tasks, time, systems, or interventions.

## 6.6 Survival, reliability, and event-history models

Discovery, failure, recovery, and abandonment are naturally represented
as time-to-event or competing-risk problems. These models handle
censoring and changing hazards more appropriately than binary labels.
Recurrent-event and multi-state variants can represent repeated errors,
recovery cycles, and episode transitions.

# 7. Candidate Predictive Framework

Let an interaction episode be represented by the layered formal model
established previously. For participant x at time t, define the legally
available predictive information:

H_t = \<s_t, pi_t, O_t, Q_t, y_0:t, e_x, b_t, z_t, c_t\>

where s_t is system state; pi_t is projection; O_t is typed opportunity
structure; Q_t is authority and policy state; y_0:t is the recorded and
attributed trace up to the cutoff; e_x is measured experience; b_t is a
belief-state estimate where justified; z_t is a strategy hypothesis
distribution; and c_t is declared context.

For target Y at horizon h under prediction regime r, the predictor
produces:

p(Y\_{t+h} \| H_t, r, M, D)

where M identifies model assumptions and D identifies the training or
calibration evidence. Under an intervention a, the target becomes
p(Y\_{t+h} \| do(a), H_t, M, D). The two expressions must not be
substituted without identification assumptions.

The predictive framework contains six linked layers:

-   Target layer: target, unit, horizon, outcome definition, competing
    outcomes, and censoring.

-   Information layer: cutoff, observable variables, derived variables,
    latent estimates, and prohibited future information.

-   Model layer: predictor family, priors or regularization, update
    rule, and causal assumptions.

-   Uncertainty layer: aleatoric, epistemic, measurement,
    distributional, and structural uncertainty.

-   Evaluation layer: baselines, held-out design, calibration,
    discrimination, interval coverage, and utility.

-   Validity layer: population, task, projection, time, intervention,
    and monitoring conditions.

# 8. Causal Assumptions

Predictive accuracy does not establish a causal mechanism. Causal claims
require an explicit causal graph or structural model, temporal ordering,
intervention semantics, and assumptions concerning confounding,
selection, measurement, and interference. Four distinctions are
mandatory:

-   Prediction under observation versus prediction under intervention.

-   Individual treatment or intervention response versus average effect.

-   Mediation as a causal claim versus predictive feature contribution.

-   Transport across contexts versus ordinary cross-validation within
    one context.

The interaction domain intensifies interference: one participant\'s
action changes the state and opportunities of others; system adaptations
alter later observations; and predictive interventions may change the
target process. Static independent-and-identically-distributed
assumptions are therefore often inappropriate. Sequential causal models,
randomized interventions, natural experiments, or explicit policy
evaluation are required for intervention claims.

# 9. Uncertainty and Prediction Limits

A prediction should be a distribution, interval, set, ranked list, or
hazard unless deterministic structure is independently established.
Point predictions conceal uncertainty and invite false precision. The
framework distinguishes:

-   Aleatoric uncertainty: irreducible variation conditional on the
    model and information set.

-   Epistemic uncertainty: uncertainty about parameters, functions, or
    hypotheses due to limited evidence.

-   Measurement uncertainty: error introduced by instruments,
    segmentation, coding, and construct operationalization.

-   State uncertainty: partial observability of current system, agent,
    or social state.

-   Structural uncertainty: uncertainty over causal structure, model
    family, or latent-state representation.

-   Distributional uncertainty: uncertainty caused by population, task,
    projection, policy, or temporal shift.

-   Reflexive uncertainty: change caused by revealing or acting on a
    prediction.

Conformal prediction can provide finite-sample marginal coverage under
exchangeability, but it does not solve conditional validity, causal
transport, or nonstationary sequential interaction. Bayesian credible
intervals depend on model and prior assumptions. Ensembles estimate some
forms of model uncertainty but do not guarantee coverage. Uncertainty
claims must therefore name the guarantee and its assumptions.

Fundamental limits arise from observational equivalence, hidden goals,
underdetermined strategies, partial observability, chaotic or highly
sensitive dynamics, changing policies, endogenous learning, rare
outcomes, insufficient support for interventions, and open-world
exogenous events. In such cases the scientifically correct prediction
may be a broad set, a ranked scenario distribution, or a declaration of
non-identifiability.

# 10. Target-Specific Analysis

## 10.1 Discovery

Discovery should be predicted as a time-to-first-event process relative
to an opportunity contract. Predictors may include exposure, signaling,
search path, prior experience, modality, task state, and prior failed
attempts. Unselected available actions cannot be labeled undiscovered
without an independent awareness measure. Competing events include
successful discovery, prompted discovery, alternate-path completion, and
abandonment.

## 10.2 Opportunity

System-relative feasible, permitted, enabled, and exposed sets are often
computable rather than statistically predicted when the model is
complete. Agent-relative believed actions and expected consequences
require probabilistic estimation. Predictions should distinguish changes
in actual opportunity from changes in belief or signaling.

## 10.3 Errors

Error prediction should define the normative or task criterion, error
opportunity, and exposure time. Rare-event evaluation requires
precision-recall, calibrated risk, and cost-sensitive metrics rather
than accuracy alone. Error labels must not collapse execution failure,
goal mismatch, policy denial, misunderstanding, and system fault.

## 10.4 Recovery

Recovery prediction is conditional on an initiating disruption and the
available recovery graph. Suitable targets include time to repair,
selected recovery path, probability of escalation, and residual
consequence. Believed reversibility and actual reversibility must remain
separate.

## 10.5 Abandonment

Abandonment is a censored event, not merely absence of completion.
Models should distinguish temporary pause, session termination, task
substitution, and permanent non-return. Survival models with
time-varying covariates are preferable when the hazard changes with
progress and friction.

## 10.6 Adaptation

Adaptation prediction concerns change in policy, belief, skill, or
performance as experience accumulates. Learning curves forecast
aggregate change but can conceal strategy shifts. Hierarchical
state-space models can represent individual variation and update online.

## 10.7 Expertise

Expertise is multidimensional and domain-relative. Prediction may
classify current skill or forecast performance under familiar tasks, but
long-term expertise development requires longitudinal exposure, practice
quality, feedback, motivation, and domain structure. Demographic
variables should not stand in for measured experience.

## 10.8 Transfer

Transfer prediction requires a source-target similarity contract and a
carrier hypothesis. Predictions should estimate positive, null, or
negative source effects and uncertainty. Ordinary similarity or source
performance alone is insufficient.

## 10.9 Strategy

Strategy is latent and typically non-identifiable from one trace.
Predictive inference should return a posterior over strategy hypotheses
or next-action distributions, test alternative models, and update when
contingencies reveal discriminating behavior. A model that predicts
actions well may still misidentify strategy.

# 11. Prediction Protocol

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Step**                            **Requirement**
  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  1\. Declare target                  Define the outcome, unit, horizon,
                                      event time, censoring, and
                                      competing outcomes.

  2\. Freeze information cutoff       List every variable available at
                                      prediction time; prohibit
                                      future-derived features.

  3\. State use                       Separate scientific forecasting,
                                      diagnosis, causal intervention,
                                      control, and operational triage.

  4\. Specify population and context  Declare users or agents, task,
                                      projection, device, authority,
                                      environment, and time period.

  5\. Register baselines              Include prevalence, persistence,
                                      simple rules, human judgment, and
                                      established task models.

  6\. Select evaluation design        Use temporal, participant, task,
                                      projection, or deployment holdout
                                      appropriate to the intended claim.

  7\. Fit without leakage             Keep preprocessing, feature
                                      selection, imputation, and tuning
                                      within training folds.

  8\. Quantify uncertainty            Produce calibrated probabilities,
                                      intervals, sets, or hazards with
                                      named guarantees.

  9\. Evaluate multiple properties    Report discrimination, calibration,
                                      coverage, sharpness, utility,
                                      subgroup and context performance.

  10\. Test transport                 Evaluate across time, participants,
                                      tasks, projections, systems, and
                                      policies when those claims are
                                      intended.

  11\. Test interventions separately  Use experiments or identified
                                      causal models for claims about
                                      changing outcomes.

  12\. Monitor and update             Detect drift, recalibrate, revise
                                      the validity domain, and document
                                      model changes.

  13\. State failure conditions       Define minimum acceptable gain,
                                      calibration, coverage, and decision
                                      utility before use.

  14\. Preserve evidence lineage      Link each prediction to the
                                      interaction, behavior, and
                                      measurement contracts that
                                      generated its inputs.
  -----------------------------------------------------------------------

# 12. Evaluation and Falsification

A predictive theory of interaction should be rejected or narrowed if its
constructs provide no reproducible out-of-sample gain over simpler
baselines, if uncertainty is systematically miscalibrated, or if
performance collapses under the contexts included in its claimed
validity domain.

Evaluation must include out-of-sample prediction. In-sample fit,
significance, explained variance, and post hoc reconstruction do not
suffice. For probabilistic classification, report proper scoring rules
and calibration in addition to threshold metrics. For time-to-event
prediction, report time-dependent discrimination, calibration, and
censoring-aware scores. For sequences, report next-event and multi-step
performance with horizon-specific degradation. For decisions, report
expected utility and harm under the operational threshold.

# 13. Threats to Validity

-   Target leakage can enter through post-outcome fields, retrospective
    labels, or segmentation choices informed by the full trace.

-   Random train-test splits can overstate generalization when the
    intended use concerns new people, tasks, projections, or future
    periods.

-   Construct labels such as confusion, expertise, and strategy may be
    unreliable or circular.

-   Adaptive systems violate stationarity because predictions and
    interventions change later data.

-   Rare failures can produce misleading accuracy and unstable subgroup
    estimates.

-   Models may encode historical access, training, or policy
    inequalities and treat them as stable individual propensities.

-   Predictive success can invite unwarranted causal and psychological
    interpretation.

-   Closed-world simulations may omit exogenous events that dominate
    deployed interaction.

-   Aggregate calibration can coexist with severe conditional or
    subgroup miscalibration.

-   A benchmark can become part of the design process, causing
    overfitting to the evaluation regime.

# 14. Implications for Computational Interaction Science

Prediction provides a stronger test of the research program than
conceptual coherence alone. The established constructs should earn their
place by improving forecast quality, uncertainty, transport, or
intervention design relative to simpler state-and-trace models. Typed
opportunity variables should help predict discovery and invalid
attempts; transfer variables should improve target-context forecasts;
strategy distributions should improve contingent action prediction; and
formal interaction models should constrain impossible transitions and
support simulation.

Predictive success would not by itself establish an independent
discipline. Many fields develop predictive models of interaction. A
discipline-level claim would require cumulative laws or mechanisms,
stable validity domains, shared benchmarks, transportable models, and
explanatory or intervention gains that are not adequately supplied by
existing HCI, human factors, psychology, machine learning, control, or
systems theory.

The immediate empirical program should therefore prioritize
preregistered, multi-context forecasting studies with frozen contracts
and strong baselines. The decisive evidence is incremental, held-out
performance and calibration---not the apparent completeness of the
ontology.

# 15. Conclusion

Computational interaction supports predictive scientific theories, but
only in a scoped and plural sense. There is no evidence for universal
prediction of whole interactions or individual behavior. Strong
prediction is achievable for constrained motor and choice processes,
routine skilled performance, and near-term transitions when the task,
state, opportunity, and method are specified. Discovery, errors,
recovery, and abandonment are predictively tractable as probabilistic
event processes. Adaptation, expertise, transfer, and strategy can be
forecast only through richer longitudinal and latent-state models, and
their individual trajectories remain substantially uncertain.

The warranted contribution is a predictive architecture rather than a
new predictive primitive. It separates prediction from explanation and
intervention; defines target, horizon, information, uncertainty, and
validity; and requires held-out evaluation, calibration, transport
tests, and explicit failure conditions. Interaction becomes predictively
scientific when forecasts are reproducible, uncertainty-bearing, and
bounded by declared contracts. Where those conditions cannot be met, the
correct result is not a confident point estimate but a broad
distribution, an incomparable context, or a statement that the target is
not identified.

## E. Prediction Protocol Checklist

1\. Declare target: Define the outcome, unit, horizon, event time,
censoring, and competing outcomes.

2\. Freeze information cutoff: List every variable available at
prediction time; prohibit future-derived features.

3\. State use: Separate scientific forecasting, diagnosis, causal
intervention, control, and operational triage.

4\. Specify population and context: Declare users or agents, task,
projection, device, authority, environment, and time period.

5\. Register baselines: Include prevalence, persistence, simple rules,
human judgment, and established task models.

6\. Select evaluation design: Use temporal, participant, task,
projection, or deployment holdout appropriate to the intended claim.

7\. Fit without leakage: Keep preprocessing, feature selection,
imputation, and tuning within training folds.

8\. Quantify uncertainty: Produce calibrated probabilities, intervals,
sets, or hazards with named guarantees.

9\. Evaluate multiple properties: Report discrimination, calibration,
coverage, sharpness, utility, subgroup and context performance.

10\. Test transport: Evaluate across time, participants, tasks,
projections, systems, and policies when those claims are intended.

11\. Test interventions separately: Use experiments or identified causal
models for claims about changing outcomes.

12\. Monitor and update: Detect drift, recalibrate, revise the validity
domain, and document model changes.

13\. State failure conditions: Define minimum acceptable gain,
calibration, coverage, and decision utility before use.

14\. Preserve evidence lineage: Link each prediction to the interaction,
behavior, and measurement contracts that generated its inputs.

## F. Open Problems

-   Predictive identification of strategies under observational
    equivalence.

-   Calibrated individual prediction under sparse, nonstationary
    histories.

-   Transport across projections that preserve semantics but alter
    opportunity and measurement.

-   Prediction under adaptive interfaces where the model changes the
    data-generating process.

-   Causal prediction of assistance, explanation, and recovery
    interventions.

-   Joint uncertainty propagation from raw records through latent
    constructs to outcomes.

-   Benchmarks that preserve interaction boundaries and prevent target
    leakage.

-   Evaluation of whether the program\'s typed constructs add
    out-of-domain predictive gain.

**Comparative Interaction**

*Toward a Scientific Method for Comparing Computational Interactions*

Formal research paper

# Abstract

Comparisons of computational interactions are commonly reduced to task
time, error rate, preference, usability scores, feature counts, or
interface-level judgments. Such comparisons are scientifically
incomplete because they often fail to establish that the interactions
share a target, task, population, boundary, observation model, or
admissible comparison relation. They also collapse distinct dimensions -
semantics, interaction structure, opportunity, behavior, strategy,
accessibility, discoverability, recovery, cost, learning, and
measurement quality - into a single ranking.

This paper develops a cross-disciplinary method for comparing
computational interactions independently of implementation. It
integrates formal equivalence, process conformance, measurement theory,
human factors, accessibility, multi-criteria analysis, and the preceding
interaction-research framework. The central result is a gate-and-profile
architecture. A comparison must first pass admissibility gates
establishing declared targets, correspondence mappings, scope
conditions, measurement comparability, and uncertainty. It then produces
a typed comparison profile rather than an unqualified score. Aggregation
is permitted only when a decision purpose, weighting rule, compensation
assumptions, uncertainty treatment, and stakeholder authority are
declared.

The paper concludes that computational interactions can be compared
scientifically, but not by a universal metric. Scientific comparison
requires a comparison contract, typed evidence, dimension-specific
measures, explicit invariants, and rules for equivalence, dominance,
trade-off, and incomparability. The reusable artifacts are a comparison
ontology, taxonomy, contract, protocol, evaluation framework, scorecard,
admissible-comparison rules, and falsification matrix.

# 1. Problem Statement

A computational interaction is not identical to its implementation,
interface, trace, outcome, or user judgment. The same computational
target may be projected through a graphical interface, command language,
API, conversational system, or assistive modality. These projections may
preserve operation semantics while changing exposed actions, signaling,
path length, error recovery, auditability, motor demands, learning
requirements, and strategy.

A scientific comparison must therefore answer two questions in order.
First: are the candidate interactions comparable under a declared frame?
Second: on which dimensions are they equivalent, different, better,
worse, or incomparable? Most evaluation practice begins with the second
question and leaves the first implicit.

The primary contribution of this paper is a method that separates
comparison admissibility from comparative judgment. The method prevents
three recurring errors: comparing unlike targets as though they were
variants of one interaction; treating a metric as a complete construct;
and converting multidimensional differences into a total ranking without
an explicit decision model.

# 2. Foundations Inherited from the Research Program

The method inherits six constraints. Representation theory establishes
that a projection selectively preserves, transforms, omits, and
introduces properties. Opportunity theory separates possible, permitted,
reachable, exposed, signaled, believed, selected, executed, successful,
and reversible action relations. Interaction theory requires declared
participants, boundaries, coupling, timescale, events, transitions, and
completion. Behavior theory treats traces as evidence generated under an
observation model rather than as transparent behavior. Measurement
theory requires a declared measurand, operationalization, scale,
uncertainty, validity domain, and permissible interpretation.
Interaction-similarity theory distinguishes token identity, type
identity, typed equivalence, graded similarity, and incomparability.

These constraints jointly imply that comparison is not a single function
applied to two interfaces. It is an argument supported by mappings,
measurements, and scope conditions.

# 3. Literature Foundations

## 3.1 Formal equivalence and conformance

Formal methods compare systems relative to observables and abstraction
rules. Trace equivalence, simulation, bisimulation, testing equivalence,
refinement, and observational equivalence preserve different properties.
Process mining similarly separates fitness, precision, generalization,
and simplicity when comparing event logs and process models.
Alignment-based conformance identifies correspondences and deviations
rather than assuming event-token identity. These traditions support a
central rule: comparison relations must be typed before they are
computed.

Conformance is not the same as superiority. A trace may conform closely
to a model while imposing high human cost; a model may permit desired
behavior while also permitting unsafe or irrelevant behavior. Formal
relations therefore constrain comparison but do not exhaust it.

## 3.2 Measurement and context of use

Measurement theory requires stable representational relations,
permissible transformations, and uncertainty statements. Metrological
traceability concerns the documented chain linking results to
references. In interaction research, the relevant chain links records to
detected events, attributed behavior, derived variables, constructs, and
claims.

ISO 9241-11 defines usability relative to specified users, goals, and
contexts of use, with effectiveness, efficiency, and satisfaction as
outcomes. This supports context-indexed comparison rather than universal
interface quality. A result for one population, task, device, or
environment does not automatically transport to another.

## 3.3 Accessibility and non-compensatory requirements

Accessibility standards show why some dimensions cannot be averaged
away. WCAG separates perceivability, operability, understandability, and
robustness into testable success criteria. Failure of keyboard access or
text alternatives cannot be scientifically neutralized by faster
performance for another population. Accessibility therefore motivates
threshold, veto, and subgroup-preservation rules rather than purely
compensatory scoring.

## 3.4 Multi-criteria decision analysis

Multi-criteria decision analysis distinguishes description from
preference aggregation. Weighted sums assume commensurability and
compensation: a deficit on one criterion can be offset by strength on
another. Outranking methods permit partial orders and incomparability
when evidence, thresholds, or stakeholder priorities do not justify a
total ranking. Comparative interaction should adopt this discipline. A
scientific profile describes differences; a decision model may rank
alternatives, but the ranking is conditional on declared values and
constraints.

# 4. Comparison Ontology

  -----------------------------------------------------------------------
  **Concept**                         **Definition**
  ----------------------------------- -----------------------------------
  Comparison object                   The interaction token, type,

                                      opportunity profile, strategy, or

                                      population, context, boundary,
                                      timescale, and observation model.

  Correspondence mapping              A mapping between entities, states,
                                      operations, events, outcomes, or
                                      measurements across candidates.

  Dimension                           A typed aspect of comparison such
                                      as semantic, structural,
                                      opportunity, behavioral,
                                      accessibility, or cost.

                                      equivalent or acceptable.

# 8. Comparative Evaluation Framework

The recommended evaluation output has three layers.

Layer 1 - invariants and vetoes. These establish semantic target,
safety, authority, accessibility minima, and other non-negotiable
constraints. A candidate failing a veto is not equivalent or admissible
for the declared use, regardless of aggregate performance.

Layer 2 - typed profile. Each dimension is reported with operational
definition, estimate, uncertainty, evidence quality, and relevant
subgroup or context. This is the scientific result.

Layer 3 - optional decision synthesis. Ranking or selection may use
dominance, lexicographic rules, constrained optimization, utility
functions, or outranking. The decision rule must be separated from the
scientific profile and must disclose weights, thresholds, compensation
assumptions, and authority to set them.

# 10. Comparison Protocol

-   1\. State the decision-independent scientific question and identify
    the candidate interactions.

-   2\. Declare target semantics, task, users or agents, context,
    initial-state distribution, episode boundary, timescale, and success
    conditions.

-   3\. Instantiate an Interaction Contract, Opportunity Contract,
    Behavioral Evidence Contract, and Measurement Contract for each
    candidate.

-   4\. Construct correspondence mappings for entities, states,
    operations, events, outcomes, strategies, and measures. Mark
    one-to-many, ambiguous, and unmapped elements.

-   5\. Declare invariants, admissible transformations, equivalence
    tolerances, mandatory thresholds, and veto conditions before
    examining comparative outcomes.

-   6\. Test admissibility gates. Narrow the claim or declare
    incomparability where gates fail.

-   7\. Select dimension-specific measures and justify their scales,
    directionality, uncertainty, and subgroup relevance.

-   8\. Collect or derive evidence using compatible observation and
    attribution rules. Preserve raw records and provenance.

-   9\. Estimate typed differences with uncertainty. Use equivalence
    tests for sameness claims and superiority tests only for directional
    claims.

-   10\. Report the multidimensional profile, including null,
    conflicting, and subgroup-specific results.

-   11\. Apply an optional decision rule only after the profile is
    complete. Conduct weight, threshold, and uncertainty sensitivity
    analysis.

-   12\. State validity domain, transport limits, unresolved mappings,
    alternative explanations, and falsifying evidence.

# 11. Admissible Comparison Rules

-   No comparison without a declared comparison object and reference
    frame.

-   No claim of semantic preservation from equal task completion alone.

-   No claim of behavioral preservation from identical aggregate
    outcomes alone.

-   No comparison of traces without compatible observation,
    segmentation, and attribution models.

-   No inference of strategy identity from one trace or one successful
    sequence.

-   No aggregation across dimensions without a declared decision purpose
    and compensation rule.

-   No averaging across populations when a mandatory subgroup threshold
    is relevant.

-   No accessibility credit from technical conformance alone when actual
    operability is disputed; standards and user evidence play different
    roles.

-   No cost comparison without declaring included resources, excluded
    externalities, and time horizon.

-   No equivalence claim without tolerances and adequate precision to
    support them.

-   No ranking when uncertainty intervals, missing mappings, or value
    conflicts support only a partial order.

-   Implementation independence permits different realizations, not the
    omission of implementation-mediated constraints that alter actual
    interaction.

# 12. Comparative Cases

## 12.1 GUI and command line over the same operation set

A GUI and CLI may preserve backend operations and outcomes while
differing in exposure, signaling, composition, auditability, motor
demands, memory demands, and learning cost. Semantic equivalence can
coexist with opportunity and behavioral inequivalence. Experts may
obtain lower execution cost from the CLI while novices achieve higher
discovery from the GUI. The result is typically a trade-off profile, not
a universal winner.

## 12.2 API and conversational interface

An API may expose a precisely typed operation set with explicit errors,
while a conversational interface paraphrases capabilities and may
over-signal unsupported actions. Equal successful outcomes on benchmark
tasks do not establish equivalent permission transparency,
predictability, recovery, or auditability. Unsupported conversational
claims create false-positive believed opportunities and should be
represented as a veto or severe mismatch where consequential actions are
involved.

## 12.3 Accessibility variants

Visual, auditory, tactile, and multimodal projections may preserve
target semantics while changing sequence, latency, spatial
comparability, memory burden, error detection, and recovery. Comparison
requires population- and assistive-technology-specific evidence.
Aggregate performance across users can conceal exclusion. The correct
output is a subgroup-indexed accessibility and opportunity profile.

## 12.4 Novice and expert use

The implementation and exposed operations may be identical while
believed actions, strategy, search, confidence, and recovery differ.
This is not an interface-only comparison. The reference frame must
include prior experience, and learning cost should be compared through
longitudinal or transfer-sensitive designs rather than single-session
performance alone.

## 12.5 Simulated and observed interaction

A simulation may match transition frequencies or task outcomes yet fail
to preserve causal mechanisms, adaptation, social coordination, or
measurement processes. Model-to-observation comparison must separately
report calibration, trace conformance, causal adequacy, and transport.
Simulation should not be treated as a substitute population without
validation.

# 13. Statistical and Formal Analysis

Claims of equivalence should use equivalence or non-inferiority designs
with prespecified smallest effects of interest, not failure to reject a
difference. Repeated measures, hierarchical populations, learning, and
task heterogeneity require multilevel models. Time-to-discovery and
abandonment are event-time outcomes; errors and recovery are often
recurrent events; traces may require sequence alignment, process
conformance, or probabilistic model comparison.

Multiple dimensions create multiplicity and selective-reporting risks.
Confirmatory dimensions should be preregistered. Exploratory profiles
should remain labeled as exploratory. Missingness is often informative:
an unobserved action may reflect logging limits, access barriers, or
abandonment. Uncertainty should propagate from record detection and
correspondence mappings through construct estimates and final
comparisons.

Formal equivalence can establish strong guarantees within an
abstraction, but empirical claims require validating that the
abstraction preserves the phenomena of interest. Conversely, empirical
similarity does not establish formal equivalence or causal identity.

# 14. Decision Synthesis without Conceptual Collapse

A scorecard may support decisions, but a universal interaction score is
rejected. Aggregation is appropriate only when criteria are
commensurable or a defensible value function is supplied. Weighted sums
permit compensation and can hide threshold failures. Lexicographic rules
prioritize one criterion before others. Constrained optimization
maximizes selected objectives subject to non-negotiable limits.
Outranking supports partial orders where one candidate is sufficiently
strong on important criteria without being vetoed by severe weaknesses.

Sensitivity analysis is mandatory. A decision is robust only if
reasonable variation in weights, thresholds, measurement uncertainty,
and population assumptions does not reverse it. When rankings are
unstable, the correct result is conditional preference or
incomparability, not false precision.

# 16. Threats to Validity

The framework is broad and may appear to solve comparison by requiring
extensive declarations. Its value therefore depends on demonstrating
improved reproducibility, error detection, and decision quality relative
to simpler evaluation reports. Some comparisons will remain
underdetermined because goals, values, or correspondence mappings are
contested. This is not necessarily methodological failure;
incomparability may be the scientifically correct result.

Construct proliferation is another risk. The taxonomy should be reduced
when dimensions are empirically redundant under a declared domain.
Conversely, low correlations do not automatically prove conceptual
independence because instruments may be unreliable or contexts
heterogeneous.

The framework also risks privileging interactions with enumerable tasks
and state spaces. Open-ended creative, social, and institutional
interactions may require interpretive or qualitative comparisons
alongside formal and quantitative evidence. Such evidence remains
admissible when its observation, coding, reflexivity, and inference
rules are explicit.

Finally, implementation independence has limits. Rendering latency,
hardware, modality, network behavior, and device constraints can alter
coupling, opportunity, and cost. The theory compares interactions
independently of any particular implementation language or product, but
it cannot discard implementation properties that causally alter the
phenomenon.

# 17. Conclusion

Computational interactions can be compared scientifically when
comparison is treated as a structured evidential argument rather than a
feature checklist or universal score. The minimum method is a
gate-and-profile architecture.

First, admissibility gates establish a shared target, boundary,
opportunity structure, observation model, measurement system,
correspondence mapping, and ethical or accessibility constraints.
Second, a typed profile compares semantic preservation, interaction
structure, opportunity, behavior, strategy, accessibility,
discoverability, reversibility, performance cost, learning cost, and
measurement quality. Third, an optional decision model may aggregate or
rank only after its values, thresholds, compensation assumptions, and
uncertainty are declared.

The central conclusion is therefore conditional but positive: a general
scientific method for comparative interaction is justified. It is not a
universal metric and does not imply that every pair of interactions is
comparable. Its scientific strength lies in making equivalence,
difference, trade-off, dominance, and incomparability explicit and
reproducible.
